title: "Balancing weights against maximum likelihood propensity scores: a simulation study of `balnet` across sample size, overlap, dimension and penalty choice"

abstract: |
  Maximum likelihood fits propensity scores to predict treatment, balancing weights to balance covariates directly.
  `balnet` fits balancing weights by a lasso-penalised balancing loss whose path runs to exact balance or stops short where infeasible.
  We compare `balnet` with cross-validated lasso MLE weights, alone and augmented, by simulation across sample size, overlap, dimension past $p = n$, confounder density and outcome signal, with and without misspecification.
  Balancing weights have lower RMSE throughout, by a third to two thirds on average, except noisy outcomes and the poorest overlap.
  Whether the path reaches exact balance decides what else helps.
  Augmentation adds nothing there and restores the lead where it stops short.
  A second study finds stopping inside the path lowers RMSE for noisy outcomes or, once augmented, limited overlap.
  Cross-validating the balancing loss captures this most often, though none is best in more than three cells in ten.
  We recommend augmented balancing weights tuned this way.

  *Keywords:* balancing weights; propensity score; inverse probability weighting; lasso; Monte Carlo simulation.

# Introduction

Much of the evidence on programmes, treatments and interventions is observational. Without randomisation, the groups compared differ in their pre-treatment characteristics, and those differences, not the treatment, may explain any gap in outcomes.

The standard approach is to assume conditional independence, meaning that once the relevant pre-treatment characteristics are controlled for, treatment allocation is as good as random. Key to this is the propensity score, the probability of receiving treatment given the observed covariates [@rosenbaum1983]. One use of the score is inverse-propensity weighting (IPW), which weights each unit by the inverse of its estimated probability of the treatment it received. In medical research its use has increased rapidly, for example in comparing treatments from hospital records where patients were never randomised [@austin2015; @benmichaelkeel2023]. In economics, IPW is used to evaluate programmes such as job training, where the effect on participants' earnings must be recovered from a non-experimental comparison group [@busso2014].

In practice the score is unknown and must be estimated. The usual estimator is logistic regression fit by maximum likelihood (MLE). It chooses the parameters of the propensity model so that the fitted score predicts the observed treatment assignment as well as possible [@wager2024]. The goal of weighting here however, is not to predict treatment assignment accurately but to balance covariates for comparable treatment groups [@zhao2019].

While IPW with the oracle propensity score balances covariate means exactly, MLE-estimated propensity scores do not generally achieve this, even without model misspecification [@wager2024; @sverdrup2026]. Under misspecification or in small samples, small estimation errors are amplified by inversion of the propensity score and can produce severe imbalance and biased estimates [@benmichael2021]. This problem is compounded by weight instability, as observations with small propensity scores receive disproportionately large weights, inflating variance and leading researchers to ad hoc solutions [@chattopadhyay2020]. Furthermore, these fixes presume a balance check that in a review of applied medical studies using IPW, most did not make [@austin2015].

Instead of modelling the score, covariate balancing methods choose the weights to target directly the balance that IPW requires. The covariate balancing propensity score (CBPS) applies this within a propensity model, selecting its parameters to satisfy the sample balance conditions [@imai2014]. As a result, their estimates tend to be more robust to model misspecification and more efficient than those from MLE weights [@chattopadhyay2020]. Under a correctly specified linear outcome and logistic propensity model, this efficiency is exact and IPW with balancing weights is $\sqrt{n}$-consistent with lower variance than even the oracle IPW [@wager2024].

The theoretical case for covariate balancing is well established, but most implementations struggle with large or high-dimensional data. CBPS and entropy balancing approaches both enforce exact balance conditions, which become unworkable in large-scale data settings [@fong2022; @sverdrup2026]. Stable balancing weights from @zubizarreta2015 require a maximum imbalance tolerance to be set before estimation and must be re-solved if this tolerance is unattainable or the bias-variance tradeoff is unattractive [@sverdrup2026]. @zhao2019 shows balancing estimators can generally be expressed as minimising a covariate balancing loss function, which opens them to lasso and other penalties. RCAL from @tan2020a implements lasso regularisation for a covariate balancing loss function, but as the package is written in R it struggles computationally with large data.

Like balancing approaches, doubly robust estimators offer protection against misspecification. These estimators, referred to as augmented estimators, combine the weights with an outcome model and remain consistent if either the propensity model or the outcome model is correctly specified [@ding2023]. The standard version is the augmented IPW (AIPW) estimator. It corrects the regression estimate by applying the IPW weights to the outcome model's residuals and adding their average [@robins1994]. Where exact balance is out of reach, AIPW has outperformed unaugmented balancing weights [@athey2018].

Much recent work builds doubly robust estimators for the balancing approach, many obtaining the weights by optimising for balance directly rather than by first estimating a propensity score [@wang2020; @hirshberg2021; @brunssmith2025]. These augmented estimators therefore sit outside the class of covariate balancing propensity scores that @zhao2019 unifies. Within that class, Tan's augmented estimator fits the outcome model with weights from the same propensity score, so changing the weights changes the outcome model too [@tan2020b].[^1] @brunssmith2025 discuss a general augmented balancing weight (ABW) estimator, where the outcome model is held fixed and the IPW weights are replaced by balancing weights. Here, when both models are linear in the same covariates, ABW is a single regression combining the outcome model and OLS, which collapses to OLS at exact balance [@wager2024]. For weights from the covariate balancing loss above, which come through a logistic link, this collapse holds only up to an approximation error.

[^1]: Tan's estimator refits the outcome model whenever the weights change, so a comparison between weights would also be a comparison between outcome models. Applying it here would confound Study 1, which compares across weighting estimators.

Of the balancing implementations above, `balnet` from @sverdrup2026 applies modern optimisation techniques to the regularised covariate balancing loss. Like RCAL it uses lasso regularisation, but through a core solver written in C++ that scales to large and high-dimensional data. The solver also supports ridge and elastic net penalties, which Study 2 uses. Its path for $n = 100{,}000$ and $p = 500$ computes in under a minute, while alternative balancing packages failed to produce results within an hour. Under lasso regularisation the penalty parameter $\lambda$ is equivalent to the maximum allowable covariate imbalance, so its regularisation path provides a practical diagnostic for overlap and lets the analyst set the imbalance to tolerate [@sverdrup2026]. The path ends at the target imbalance rather than at exact balance, and truncates earlier where that target is infeasible. The imbalance left over can then be handed to an outcome model [@wager2024].

For modelling approaches it is standard practice to choose $\lambda$ by cross-validation (CV) of the prediction error, a choice one would reasonably expect to extend to balancing loss approaches.[^2] However, for balancing weights recent work cautions against applying cross-validation naively, finding that no tuning rule is uniformly best [@brunssmith2025].

[^2]: Both RCAL and `balnet` provide a CV setting with tunable folds in their base package.

For balancing methods the held-out loss becomes the balancing loss or the remaining covariate imbalance. CV then assumes the held-out loss is an unbiased estimate of the error in the estimated effect, but the penalty trades observable variance against unobservable bias, a trade CV cannot reliably make [@tan2020a; @brunssmith2025; @athey2018]. Following the reasoning behind balancing weights, @wang2020 score balance on bootstrap samples over a grid of approximate balance tolerances and find that under poor overlap exact balance is not always optimal. On the `balnet` path this becomes a question of where to set $\lambda$, or whether to set it at all, as by construction its truncated path already produces approximate balancing weights when exact balance is not feasible.

Study 1 asks to what degree and when balancing weights improve on MLE weights, whether used alone or in an augmented estimator. Study 2 then asks where `balnet`'s path endpoint does not minimise root mean squared error (RMSE), and whether at those points any selector beats it. Across both studies the dividing line is whether the `balnet` path reaches exact balance, which with the outcome signal tells the analyst when balancing weights, augmentation and a selector each pay.

# Aims

## Study 1

Our first study aims to guide the choice between balancing weights and MLE weights, whether used alone or in an augmented estimator. The settings that follow vary the sample size, overlap, dimension, the number and correlation of confounders, and the strength of the outcome signal. Each is run under both a correctly specified and a misspecified propensity score. Following @tan2020a, we focus on how the two sets of weights perform relative to each other across these settings and over three outcome functions.

Both sets of weights are also augmented with the same lasso outcome model, so ABW and AIPW differ only in their weights. Comparing the two shows whether differences between balancing and MLE weights hold once an outcome model is added. At exact balance, `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ differs from OLS by the approximation error of its logistic weights [@brunssmith2025]. We track this error where OLS can be fitted and the path reaches its target.

**Sample size:** Under a correctly specified propensity score both approaches are consistent [@wager2024]. For a linear outcome, IPW with balancing weights is expected to have lower variance than even IPW with the true propensity score. Here we ask how the sample size affects the relative performance of `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ and `cv.glmnet`, a baseline for the later comparisons.

Under a misspecified propensity score, IPW estimators can converge away from the true estimand, and with MLE weights their bias and RMSE have been found to worsen as $n$ grows [@warp2023; @kang2007]. We therefore ask whether the bias of `cv.glmnet` settles as $n$ rises to $10^6$, and how `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ compares. We also track AIPW, which has been found to compound errors when both models are wrong [@kang2007]. Where a bias settles while the sampling error shrinks, coverage must collapse with $n$, which we report at the empirical SE [@morris2019].

**Overlap:** We then compare the two sets of weights as overlap degrades, meaning that treated and control units increasingly lack counterparts with similar propensity scores. We also include levels at which overlap is practically violated, as defined in the data-generating mechanism.

With a correctly specified outcome model, AIPW has outperformed unaugmented approximate balancing weights at both overlap levels studied [@athey2018]. Under poor overlap and a misspecified outcome model, however, unaugmented approximate balancing weights have produced lower RMSE than AIPW [@chattopadhyay2020]. Besides these swapped signs, we ask how `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ performs once exact balance is out of reach, as exact balancing weights can become infeasible under poor overlap [@hainmueller2012; @sverdrup2026].

**High-dimensional settings:** In healthcare especially, propensity scores are fitted to a large number of covariates, as in database studies [@wyss2026]. By raising the number of covariates to $p/n = 4$ we cover these settings, which force the MLE weights to select four confounders within thousands of covariates and the balancing weights to balance thousands. Here we also ask how the balancing loss behaves as $p$ grows.

Firstly, exact balance is expected to fail for `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ around $p/n = 0.5$, so that its path stops short of its target. Here, we look for the error of `cv.glmnet` to grow gradually with $p$ [@tan2020b], and for ABW to separate from `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ [@wager2024]. Against AIPW, augmented balancing weights have kept a lead in past work, though not one that consistently widened with $p$ [@athey2018; @Ninget.al], so we also examine this lead.

Secondly, we ask whether misspecification changes how the modelling estimators respond to added covariates. Under misspecification, the RMSE of IPW with MLE weights fell as $p$ grew in @tan2017 but rose in @athey2018. Running both specifications on the same draws lets us consider the effects of $p$ and misspecification separately.

**With a denser covariate profile:** The $p/n$ grid is limited to four confounders, as Kang–Schafer misspecification requires [@kang2007]. This is restrictive, as conditional independence typically needs many covariates to be plausible. Here, we increase the number of confounders $s$ to $16$ and $64$, allow their signal to even out as the decay rate $\nu$ falls from $1$ to $0.5$, and consider independent, AR(1)-correlated and equicorrelated covariance structures. Each design also has a misspecified propensity score, built from the transformation of @tan2020b. There, balancing weights from the same loss as `balnet` have substantially outperformed MLE weights [@tan2020a], which we test at every $s$.

At $p/n = 0.1$, the error from modelling weights is bounded at a rate that grows with the number of active covariates [@tan2020b]. In contrast, exact balancing weights give an unbiased estimate for a linear outcome at any $s$ [@benmichael2021]. The advantage of balancing over modelling weights should then widen as $s$ rises. From $p/n = 0.5$, however, exact balance should fail, and the bias of balancing weights for a linear outcome is then at most the largest remaining imbalance scaled by the $\ell_1$ norm of the outcome coefficients [@zhao2019]. As the outcome signal has fixed variance, spreading it over more confounders raises this norm, so the bias should rise with $s$ and as $\nu$ falls, except under equicorrelation. Correlation may pull the other way. When the outcome variance is held fixed, correlated confounders absorb part of each other's signal and their coefficients shrink, lowering the $\ell_1$ norm that bounds the bias, most of all under equicorrelation.

Raising $s$ also makes the propensity model denser, which matters for the augmented estimators. AIPW relies on a sufficiently sparse propensity model, whereas augmented balancing weights assume nothing about treatment assignment beyond overlap [@athey2018]. AIPW should then lose ground to ABW as that model grows denser.

**Outcome signal:** Lastly, we ask how the strength of the outcome signal changes the comparison between balancing and modelling weights. Here, the outcome signal strength $\kappa$ rises from $0.02$ to $1$ against a fixed noise level, under both correctly specified and misspecified propensity scores.

As $\kappa$ falls, the bias that exact balance removes shrinks, but its cost in variance does not. At low $\kappa$, `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ may then lose ground to modelling weights. At larger $\lambda$ its path gives approximate balance, which lets us choose how much bias to trade for variance, though the best trade depends on the signal-to-noise ratio [@wang2020; @zhao2019].

## Study 2

In preliminary runs a cross-validated $\lambda$ beat the path endpoint for IPW only when the outcome signal was weak. Our second study therefore asks whether tuning or bootstrapping approaches can offer a better stopping point than the endpoint. First, when does the RMSE-minimising $\lambda$ come before the path endpoint, an interior optimum. Second, where and how often does one of our five selectors improve on the endpoint, a selector win.

By construction no selector sees the outcome, so each picks the $\lambda$ on the path that minimises one of three criteria. The first, `bloss`, is the balancing loss that `balnet` minimises along its path. The second, `smd`, is the mean absolute standardised mean difference across covariates after weighting, the bootstrap balance measure of @wang2020 averaged rather than summed. The third, `inf`, is the largest absolute standardised mean difference after weighting, the quantity our $\lambda$ bounds under lasso.

Each criterion is scored by cross-validation or by a half-sample bootstrap motivated by @wang2020. The balancing loss is scored by cross-validation only, giving five selectors, as its fit minimises its own target and scoring it on sub-samples would favour the endpoint deterministically, analogous to scoring a likelihood at its own maximiser.

We are especially interested in overlap and outcome signal. Approximate balance has been found to lower RMSE relative to exact balance when overlap is limited [@wang2020]. For augmented balancing weights with ridge penalties, the RMSE-minimising penalty has been found to grow with outcome noise, which selectors using only the covariates and treatment cannot see [@brunssmith2025]. If this holds for `balnet`, interior optima and selector wins should both become more likely as $\kappa$ falls. We also ask whether moving the penalty form $\alpha$ from lasso towards ridge lowers RMSE, at the endpoint or at the interior optimum.

# Methods

## Estimand

Our estimand is the average treatment effect, $\tau = \mathbb{E}[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)]$. We set $\tau = 0$ in every cell so $\hat \tau$ is its own error by construction.

## Data-generating mechanism

**Simulation design:** We combine data-generating process (DGP) designs from the IPW literature into one model that reproduces the stress conditions common in observational data. The design of @kang2007, extended to high-dimensional settings by @tan2020a, provides our baseline for testing misspecification. As overlap is a key assumption of IPW, an overlap scaler on the propensity score gives a range of overlap conditions [@busso2014; @keele2025]. While the design of @tan2020a is high-dimensional, only four of its covariates are active. A sparsity parameter, as in @zhao2019, allows the more realistic case where many covariates are active. Autoregressive covariance structures, as in @tan2020b and @zhao2019, allow simulation under moderate correlation, and an equicorrelated structure extends that correlation to every covariate. Finally, since a comparison of RMSE depends on the sample size, we vary it [@morris2019].

Within this design, each cell draws $n$ observations of $p$ multivariate normal covariates $X_i = (X_{i1}, \ldots, X_{ip})$ with mean zero and unit variance. Their covariance takes three levels. Setting $\operatorname{cov}(X_{ij}, X_{ik}) = \rho^{|j-k|}$ gives iid covariates at $\rho = 0$ and an AR(1) structure at $\rho = 0.5$, and a third, equicorrelated level sets $\operatorname{cov}(X_{ij}, X_{ik}) = 0.5$ for all $j \neq k$ through one common factor, $X_{ij} = \sqrt{0.5}\,Z_{i0} + \sqrt{0.5}\,Z_{ij}$ with $Z_{i0}, Z_{ij} \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ [@friedman2010]. Under AR(1) the active covariates are adjacent, which may limit the effect of correlation [@athey2018], whereas under equicorrelation every inactive covariate shares the common factor with the active ones. The treated proportion is 0.5, as in @kang2007.

The true propensity score is $$e^*(X_i) = \left\{1 + \exp\left(\frac{g_i}{c\,\sigma_g} - \alpha\right)\right\}^{-1},
\qquad g_i = \sum_{j=1}^{s} j^{-\nu} X_{ij},$$ {#eq-score} where $s$ is the number of active covariates, $\nu$ is their signal decay rate along $j$ and $\alpha$ sets the treated proportion. Overlap holds for any overlap scaler $c > 0$, with $c = 1$ as its base to roughly correspond with @tan2020a.[^3] Lowering $c$ weakens overlap by pushing $e^*(X_i)$ towards 0 and 1.

[^3]: The design in @tan2020a corresponds to $c = 1/1.15 \approx 0.87$ so our base case has slightly stronger overlap levels, due to our standardisation.

@atbl-ov-levels shows the proportion of units whose true propensity score falls outside \[0.01, 0.99\] and \[0.05, 0.95\] at each level of $c$, and @afig-ov-levels displays the density of $e^*(X_i)$ for each arm. In the terms of @wager2024, our design satisfies weak but not strong overlap, as $e^*(X_i)$ stays strictly between 0 and 1 at any $c > 0$ but is never bounded away from them. Under sufficiently degraded overlap, samples contain covariate regions with only treated or only control units, which we consider practical violations of common support following @chattopadhyay2020. Such violations are possible at $c=0.5$, likely at $0.25$ and almost certain by $c \le 0.05$.

To prevent changes in $s$, $\nu$ and the covariance structure shifting overlap, we standardise $g_i$ using its population variance $\sigma_g^2 = \sum_{j,k \le s} (jk)^{-\nu} \operatorname{cov}(X_{ij}, X_{ik})$. Dividing by $\sigma_g$ makes $g_i/\sigma_g$ standard normal, leaving only $c$ and $\alpha$ to shift $e^*(X_i)$. To prevent $c$ shifting the treated proportion, we select $\alpha$ numerically so that the expected value of $e^*(X_i)$ equals the target, which gives $\alpha = 0$ at 0.5[^4]. Treatment is assigned as $W_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}\{e^*(X_i)\}$. Potential outcomes are generated as $Y_i(0) = Y_i(1) = \kappa\, h(X_i) + \varepsilon_i$, where $\varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ and $\kappa$ sets the outcome signal strength, so at $\kappa = 0$ the outcome is noise alone. Outcome specifications follow @tan2020a and use the first four covariates, the active set when $s = 4$, $$\begin{aligned}
h^{\text{lin}}(X_i)  &= X_{i1} + 0.5\,X_{i2} + 0.5\,X_{i3} + 0.5\,X_{i4} \\
h^{\text{quad}}(X_i) &= \sum_{j=1}^{4} \{\max(X_{ij}, 0)\}^2 \\
h^{\text{exp}}(X_i)  &= \sum_{j=1}^{4} \exp(X_{ij}/2)
\end{aligned}$$ {#eq-outcomes} In the sparsity grid, to keep every active covariate a confounder as $s$ varies, we instead let $h$ load on all $s$ active covariates, weighted by $j^{-\nu}$.

[^4]: Since $g_i/\sigma_g$ is standard normal, this mean depends only on $\alpha$ and $c$ and rises strictly in $\alpha$, so the solution is unique and found by `uniroot.`

**Misspecification structure:** We force misspecification with the covariate transformations of @kang2007, in which the estimators observe transformed covariates $\tilde{X}$ rather than the true $X$, $$\begin{aligned}
\tilde{X}_{i1} &= \exp(X_{i1}/2) \\
\tilde{X}_{i2} &= \frac{X_{i2}}{1 + \exp(X_{i1})} + 10 \\
\tilde{X}_{i3} &= (0.04\,X_{i1}\,X_{i3} + 0.6)^3 \\
\tilde{X}_{i4} &= (X_{i2} + X_{i4} + 20)^2 .
\end{aligned}$$ {#eq-ks} As in @tan2020a, $\tilde{X}_{i1}, \ldots, \tilde{X}_{i4}$ are standardised within each sample to mean zero and unit variance, and the remaining covariates are observed as they are. The transformations are written for four covariates, so we apply them at $s = 4$, where the transformed covariates are exactly the confounders shared by $e^*(X_i)$ and $Y_i$.

These transformations misspecify both models our augmented estimators fit, a logistic score and a linear outcome model. Here, the data-generating score and outcome do not change. They are still a logit and a linear regression in $X$, and written in the observed $\tilde{X}$ they remain linear in the parameters with nonlinear terms in $\tilde{X}$. The estimators are misspecified only in that they enter the transformed covariates themselves as the linear terms. This gives a realistic misspecification structure, in which a slight error in a researcher's functional form is enough to misspecify a model [@kang2007].

::: {#tbl-spec}
| Arm | $\hat{e}$ on | Outcome on | $\hat{e}$ | Outcome linear | Outcome nonlinear |
|------------|:----------:|:----------:|:----------:|:----------:|:----------:|
| Correct specification | $X$ | $X$ | correct | correct | misspecified |
| Misspecification | $\tilde{X}$ | $\tilde{X}$ | misspecified | misspecified | misspecified |
| Refit on $X$ (`_ortrue`) | $\tilde{X}$ | $X$ | misspecified | correct | misspecified |

Specification of the propensity score and the outcome model in each arm of the design, by outcome.
:::

Only the augmented estimators have an outcome model, so only they reach the third row of @tbl-spec. There the outcome model is refitted on $X$ and is correct, so its residuals have mean zero and weighting them with a misspecified score adds no bias. The second row is the case @kang2007 describe as the practical motivation behind doubly robust estimators, where a practitioner naturally assumes a linear outcome model and a logistic score are adequate because both look trustworthy. There, naive application of doubly robust estimators can give errors that grow with sample size, which we call double fragility, following @testa2026.

Beyond $s = 4$ the Kang–Schafer transformations no longer reach every confounder, so our denser grids use the transformation of @tan2020b instead. Here, $X^\dagger_{ij} = X_{ij} + \{\max(X_{ij} + 1, 0)\}^2$ is applied to every active covariate and standardised within each sample, while $W_i$ and $Y_i$ are still generated from $X$. To keep the same practical interpretation of misspecification, we deviate from @tan2020b by placing $X^\dagger$ in the observed covariates rather than the true models. Both models fitted on $X^\dagger$ are then misspecified, as before.

**Simulation settings:** Each grid varies one or more factors against a base case of $n = 1000$, $p = 50$, $s = 4$, $\nu = 1$, $\rho = 0$, $c = 1$, $\kappa = 1$ and a treated proportion of 0.5, with all three outcomes computed on each draw. Most grids vary one factor (@tbl-grids). Sample size is crossed with overlap, dimension, path endpoint and treated proportion, and the denser grids cross five factors, a non-factorial structure chosen for computational time [@morris2019]. Within a grid every estimator and both specifications run on the same draws, from L'Ecuyer–CMRG streams indexed by cell and replication, so only the observed covariates differ between the correct and misspecified arms. Cells use 10 000 replications, except 1000 on the $n \times c$ and denser grids, with Monte Carlo standard errors on every measure, and a replication in which an estimator fails is kept as missing and counted [@morris2019]. All runs use R 4.5 or 4.6 [@rcore2025] with `balnet` 0.0.4 [@sverdrup2026] and `glmnet` 5.0 [@friedman2010]. The code, run scripts and stored summaries are available from the author.


### Study 2

Study 2 changes two things in the design of Study 1. Here, each replication carries seven outcomes on one draw, with $\kappa$ halved from one to $1/32$ and then set to zero, so the selectors, folds and half-samples are shared along the noise axis. The penalty form $\alpha$ runs from ridge through the elastic net to lasso. Overlap takes six of the seven values of Study 1, without $c = 2$. Sample size, dimension and misspecification are each crossed with overlap, and $n$ and $p$ with $\alpha$ as well. A denser grid takes the confounder profile $s \in \{4, 16, 64\}$ under its three covariance structures, at $n = 1000$, $p = 100$ and $c = 0.25$ under both specifications. Every grid runs 2500 replications except the two largest samples at 1000 (@tbl-grids-s2).

## Methodology

We consider the standard potential outcomes setting with a sample of $n$ units, a treatment indicator $W_i \in \{0, 1\}$ and potential outcomes $Y_i(1)$ and $Y_i(0)$ under treatment and control. Identification of the ATE, $\tau = \mathbb{E}[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)]$, relies on conditional independence and overlap. Under these assumptions the propensity score $e(x) = P[W_i = 1 \mid X_i = x]$ allows unbiased estimation via IPW:

$$\tau = \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{W_i Y_i}{e(X_i)} - \frac{(1 - W_i) Y_i}{1 - e(X_i)}\right].$$ {#eq-ipw}

**Propensity score estimation:** We compare two approaches under a logistic propensity score model, $e(x) = 1 / [1 + \exp\{-(\beta_0 + x^\top \beta)\}]$. Both use penalised logistic regression but differ in the loss function minimised.

**Standard MLE approach:** The MLE approach estimates $\beta$ by minimising the negative Bernoulli log-likelihood, $$\ell_{\text{ML}}(\beta) = -\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[ W_i \eta_i - \log\{1 + \exp(\eta_i)\} \right],$$ {#eq-mle} where $\eta_i = \beta_0 + X_i^\top \beta$. This targets accurate prediction of treatment assignment, with first-order conditions $$\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \{ W_i - \hat{e}(X_i) \} X_{ij} = 0, \quad j = 1, \ldots, p,$$ {#eq-mle-foc} that balance predicted and observed treatment whatever the specification. We use the penalised MLE of the `glmnet` package [@friedman2010], which computes a regularisation path in a penalty parameter $\lambda$ that acts as a coefficient budget, with lasso penalties and $\lambda$ chosen by five-fold cross-validation at its minimum-deviance value, the estimator we write `cv.glmnet`.

**Covariate balancing approach:** The covariate balancing approach starts from the finite-sample bias of IPW estimators, which is driven by covariate imbalance [@wager2024, ch. 7]. Achieving this balance in finite samples requires $$\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{W_i X_{ij}}{\hat{e}(X_i)} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_{ij}, \quad j = 1, \ldots, p.$$ {#eq-exactbalance}

For estimating treatment effects the covariate balancing approach uses two separate fits, targeting balance for the treated and control means. When estimating the treated mean $\mathbb{E}[Y_i(1)]$, this balance condition is enforced by a loss function with first-order conditions $$\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( \frac{W_i}{\hat{e}(X_i)} - 1 \right) X_{ij} = 0, \quad j = 1, \ldots, p,$$ {#eq-bal-foc} which integrates to the covariate balancing loss function $$\ell_1(\eta) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[ W_i \exp(-\eta_i) + (1 - W_i) \eta_i \right].$$ {#eq-bal-loss} The corresponding loss function $\ell_0(\eta)$ for the control mean $\mathbb{E}[Y_i(0)]$ follows by symmetry. For exact balancing, the condition for a solution to exist is also stricter under this approach than with MLE, requiring that no linear combination of the covariates is non-negative on every treated unit while averaging at or below zero over the controls [@tan2020a]. To address this, we regularise the covariate balancing loss function using the penalised approach of @sverdrup2026, where the penalised objective under lasso regularisation is

$$\ell_1(\eta) + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{p} |\beta_j|.$$ {#eq-bal-pen} Under lasso penalisation, the exact balance requirements from @eq-exactbalance are relaxed by the KKT conditions giving

$$\left| \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{W_i X_{ij}}{\hat{e}(X_i)} - \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} X_{ij} \right| \leq \lambda, \quad j = 1, \ldots, p.$$ {#eq-kkt}

Here $\lambda$ is the maximum allowable imbalance across covariates, in standardised mean differences since `balnet` standardises the covariates by default. The regularisation path then gives a sequence of solutions at decreasing imbalance tolerances, which also serves as a diagnostic for overlap [@sverdrup2026]. When further reductions in imbalance are infeasible, `balnet` truncates its path before the path floor $\lambda_{min} = 10^{-4}$, and we count a replication as truncated when either arm's path ends above it. The estimator at the path end is written `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$. In the terms of @zhao2019, `balnet` is then an approximate balancing estimator, defined by the imbalance left in each arm, bounded by $\lambda$.[^5]

[^5]: For $\alpha < 1$, used in Study 2, each covariate's imbalance is no longer capped and grows with its coefficient, moving `balnet` from the lasso's control of the worst covariate toward $\ell_2$ ridge balancing [@brunssmith2025].

**Modelling IPW estimators:** Modelling aims for covariate balance by predicting the propensity score, on the intuition that a correctly estimated propensity score will balance confounders through IPW estimation.

1.  The Horvitz–Thompson (HT) IPW estimator for the ATE,

    $$\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\frac{W_iY_i}{\hat e(X_i)} - \frac{(1-W_i)Y_i}{1-\hat e(X_i)}\right],$$ {#eq-ht}

    weights each unit by the inverse of its estimated propensity score $\hat e(X_i)$, following the survey sampling estimator from @horvitz1952. Under the oracle propensity score it is unbiased for $\tau$ [@wager2024, ch. 2].

2.  The Hájek (H) estimator, $$\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H}} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} W_iY_i/\hat e(X_i)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} W_i/\hat e(X_i)} - \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (1-W_i)Y_i/\{1-\hat e(X_i)\}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (1-W_i)/\{1-\hat e(X_i)\}},$$ {#eq-hajek} normalises the HT estimator by dividing both groups by the sum of their weights, bounding the estimate by the observed outcomes to avoid minor errors in $\hat e(X_i)$ causing large errors in $\hat\tau$ through inversion [@hajek1971; @ding2023, ch. 11].

For the balancing loss approach there is no distinction between HT and H, as the weights in each arm sum to $n$ by construction when the balancing loss is minimised [@tan2020a; @sverdrup2026]. Three references complete the set. The oracle is each estimator at the true propensity score, OLS is fitted within each arm on the observed covariates and predicted for all units [@kang2007], and the unadjusted estimator is the difference in means.

**Doubly robust IPW estimators:** To mitigate the effects of model misspecification, both doubly robust estimators estimate an outcome model alongside the propensity score, as only one need be correctly specified.

1.  The augmented IPW (AIPW) estimator [@robins1994].

    $$\begin{aligned}
    \hat\tau_{\mathrm{AIPW}} ={}& \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl[\hat m_1(X_i) - \hat m_0(X_i)\bigr] \\
    &+ \frac{\sum_{i}\hat w_i^{(1)}\{Y_i - \hat m_1(X_i)\}}{\sum_{i}\hat w_i^{(1)}}
    - \frac{\sum_{i}\hat w_i^{(0)}\{Y_i - \hat m_0(X_i)\}}{\sum_{i}\hat w_i^{(0)}},
    \end{aligned}$$ {#eq-aipw}

    adds a penalised outcome model to the MLE weights. The outcome model $\hat m_w(x) = \hat\beta_{w,0} + x^\top\hat\beta_w$ estimates $m_w(x) = \mathbb{E}[Y_i(w) \mid X_i = x]$, and is fit within arm $w$ and predicted for all $n$ units. Residual terms are normalised as in the Hájek estimator [@ding2023]. The population bias for $\mu_1 = \mathbb{E}[Y_i(1)]$ is the product of the two models' errors,

    $$\operatorname{Bias}(\hat\mu_1^{\mathrm{AIPW}}) = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{e(X) - \hat e(X)}{\hat e(X)}\,\{m_1(X) - \hat m_1(X)\}\right],$$ {#eq-aipw-bias}

    so one correct model is enough. In finite samples the error is bounded by the product of the two fits' errors, so with both models misspecified neither factor is small and the errors can compound [@ding2023].

2.  The augmented balancing weights (ABW) estimator, in the general form of @brunssmith2025, is for the ATE $$\begin{aligned} \hat\tau_{\mathrm{ABW}} ={}& \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl[\hat m_1(X_i) - \hat m_0(X_i)\bigr] \\ &+ \frac{\sum_{i}\hat\gamma_i^{(1)}\{Y_i - \hat m_1(X_i)\}}{\sum_{i}\hat\gamma_i^{(1)}} - \frac{\sum_{i}\hat\gamma_i^{(0)}\{Y_i - \hat m_0(X_i)\}}{\sum_{i}\hat\gamma_i^{(0)}}, \end{aligned}$$ {#eq-abw} where $\hat\gamma_i^{(1)}, \hat\gamma_i^{(0)}$ are the `balnet` weights at the path endpoint and $\hat m_w(x) = \hat\beta_{w,0} + x^\top\hat\beta_w$ is a lasso outcome model fit within arm $w$ through the cross-validated penalty parameter $\delta_w$, predicted for all $n$ units.

    @brunssmith2025 show that with weights and outcome model linear in the same covariates, the ABW estimator collapses to OLS at exact balance, $$ \hat\tau_{\mathrm{ABW}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl[\hat m_1(X_i) - \hat m_0(X_i)\bigr], \qquad \lambda_1 = \lambda_0 = 0. $$ {#eq-abw-ols}

    Under lasso ($\ell_1$, $\alpha = 1$) the collapse at exact balance is the same. Away from it, the weights correct balance only for covariates whose raw imbalance exceeds $\lambda$, with $\hat m_w$ handling the rest, a closed form that holds only for uncorrelated covariates [@brunssmith2025, Prop. 5.1–5.2 and supp. App. E.3].

    The balancing weights of `balnet` are built on a logistic propensity score, so at exact balance the logistic link leaves $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{ABW}}$ an approximation error relative to OLS [@brunssmith2025, Remark 5 and supp. Prop. D.1].

## Regularisation

We fit both approaches under the elastic net framing of @friedman2010. Here $\alpha$ sets the form of the penalty, ridge at $\alpha = 0$, lasso at $\alpha = 1$ and the elastic net anywhere between. The penalty shrinks coefficients, scaled by $\lambda$, as each fit minimises $$\ell_1(\eta) + \lambda \Big[ (1 - \alpha)\tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{j=1}^{p} \beta_j^2 + \alpha \sum_{j=1}^{p} |\beta_j| \Big].$$ {#eq-enet} Ridge shrinks every coefficient towards zero leaving all nonzero, the lasso sets some at exactly zero, and the elastic net does both in a mix set by $\alpha$. Study 1 uses only the lasso penalty ($\ell_1$), while Study 2 covers all three.

## Performance measures {#sec-s1-measures}

**Bias:** the average error of the estimates, $\mathrm{Bias} = \bar\tau - \tau$, where $\bar\tau = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{r=1}^{m}\hat\tau_r$ is the mean of the estimates $\hat\tau_r$ over $m$ replications. As $\tau = 0$, bias is $\bar\tau$.

**EmpSE:** the standard deviation of the estimates across replications, $\mathrm{EmpSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{m-1}\sum_{r=1}^{m}(\hat\tau_r - \bar\tau)^2}$, measuring precision [@morris2019].

**RMSE:** the root mean squared error, $\mathrm{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{m}\sum_{r=1}^{m}(\hat\tau_r - \tau)^2}$, combining bias and precision, as $\mathrm{RMSE}^2 \approx \mathrm{Bias}^2 + \mathrm{EmpSE}^2$.

**MCSE:** the Monte Carlo standard error, the uncertainty in each measure from using a finite $m$, derived as in @morris2019. Bands and bars in the figures are 95% Monte Carlo intervals. For bias, it is $\mathrm{EmpSE}/\sqrt{m}$, for RMSE it is $\mathrm{SD}\big[(\hat\tau_r - \tau)^2\big]/(2\,\mathrm{RMSE}\sqrt{m})$ by the delta method, and for EmpSE it is $\mathrm{EmpSE}/\sqrt{2(m-1)}$.

**Coverage at the empirical SE:** the share $C$ of replications in which $\hat\tau_r \pm 1.96\,\mathrm{EmpSE}$ covers $\tau$, with Monte Carlo standard error $\sqrt{C(1 - C)/m}$. No variance estimator is implemented for the balancing weights, so EmpSE stands in for the estimated width. With the width exact and the estimates near normal, bias is the only source of under-coverage, so this is the coverage a correctly sized interval would reach. Coverage at the nominal $0.95$, the level the interval claims, means the bias is small against the spread, and coverage falls with $n$ wherever the bias shrinks more slowly than $\sqrt{1/n}$ [@morris2019].

**Relative RMSE performance** $\boldsymbol{\bar R(\Theta)}$**:** To guide the choice between estimators, we introduce an average relative performance indicator $\bar R(\Theta)$. Here, estimator $A$ is compared with estimator $B$ over $\Theta$, a set of cells $c$, where each $c$ is a simulation setting under our DGP. So that cells with large RMSE do not dominate, the ratio $R_c$ is averaged on the log scale, with its exponent taken for $\bar R(\Theta)$, $$R_c = \frac{\mathrm{RMSE}_{A,c}}{\mathrm{RMSE}_{B,c}}, \qquad \bar R(\Theta) = 100\Big\{1 - \exp\Big(\frac{1}{|\Theta|} \sum_{c \in \Theta} \log R_c\Big)\Big\},$$ {#eq-rbar} so that $\bar R(\Theta) > 0$ indicates that, over $\Theta$, estimator $A$ has on average $\bar R(\Theta)$ per cent lower RMSE than $B$.

**Share of bias** $\boldsymbol{\bar s_m(\Theta)}$**:** To show whether differences in $\bar R(\Theta)$ are driven by bias or variance, for each estimator $m$ we report its share of bias using squared RMSE (MSE), $$s_{m,c} = \frac{\mathrm{bias}_{m,c}^2}{\mathrm{RMSE}_{m,c}^2}, \qquad \bar s_m(\Theta) = \frac{1}{|\Theta|}\sum_{c \in \Theta} s_{m,c}.$$ {#eq-sbar}

A cell counts as a win for $A$ when $\log R_c$ lies more than three Monte Carlo standard errors below zero, and as a loss when it lies more than three above, so cells within three MCSE of zero are ties.

By holding $\tau = 0$ fixed, comparing ratios, jointly considering $\bar R(\Theta)$ and $\bar s_m(\Theta)$, and using RMSE, which is on the same scale as EmpSE, we address several precautions raised by @morris2019.

### Study 2

**Selectors:** Each selector picks a $\lambda$ from one full `balnet` fit per replication, which also supplies the path endpoint. Cross-validation refits the path on ten folds, scores every $\lambda$ on the held-out fold and takes the $\lambda$ with the lowest mean score. The three cross-validated criteria are scored on the same folds, so they differ only in the criterion. The bootstrap does not refit. It scores the weights of the full fit on 500 random half-samples of the data and takes the $\lambda$ with the lowest mean score, following @wang2020. Selection is made separately in the treated and control fits, so a selector returns one $\lambda$ per arm.

**Evaluation:** Each selected $\lambda$ gives both balancing estimators from Study 1. Under lasso the path ends at a maximum imbalance of $10^{-4}$, as in Study 1. Under ridge and the elastic net $\lambda$ no longer bounds the standardised mean differences, so the path ends at a fixed fraction of $\lambda_{\max}$ instead. To locate the RMSE-minimising $\lambda$, both estimators are also evaluated at every point of a fixed $\lambda$ grid per cell, set from a pilot draw and spaced evenly on the log scale from $\lambda_{\max}$ to the path end.

**Measures:** Both aims are read from RMSE relative to the path endpoint on the same draws. An interior optimum occurs when the lowest RMSE along the $\lambda$ grid sits more than five per cent below the endpoint's. This is a reporting threshold, about two Monte Carlo standard errors at 2500 replications. A selector win occurs when a selector's RMSE sits below the endpoint's by more than three times their combined Monte Carlo standard error. Combining the two as if independent overstates the error of the difference, since the estimates share draws, so the rule errs towards calling a tie. Both are reported as the share of cells in which they occur, and a win carries the selector's RMSE as a ratio to the endpoint's.

**Robustness check:** Both rules are also applied, with `balnet` alone, to the design of @wongchan2018 as run by @wang2020, matched to our misspecified grid by overlap and confounding strength. The two designs give the same verdict on the selector win in every one of fifteen matched cells and on the interior optimum in all but one ([Appendix H](#sec-app-wc)).

```{r}
#| label: n-path-data
#| include: false
# balnet, glmnet (Hájek) and AIPW-glmnet along n under a misspecified

# model on the true covariates (stored section misspec_npath,
# handoff/R/sections.R): n = 250 to 200k on the fine grid's draws, and

npath_built <- file.exists(here::here("output", "thesis_summaries",
                                      "misspec_npath.rds"))
npath_arms <- c("balnet0", "abw_balnet0", "glmnetcv_hajek",
                "aipw_glmnetcv")
ortrue_arms <- c("balnet0", "abw_balnet0_ortrue", "glmnetcv_hajek",

if (npath_built) {
  misspec_npath <- read_summary("misspec_npath")
  npath_grid <- setdiff(unique(misspec_npath$perf$n), 1e6)
```
