```{r}
                                       "linear"), 2)
  # ABW-balnet leaves balnet's line at n = 250 only
  npath_abw <- signif(max(npath_gap(misspec_npath, "abw_balnet0", "balnet0",
                                    from = 500)), 1)
  # the captions are typed in the figure chunks so they read and edit as
  # text; the render stops here if the stored numbers no longer match them
  stopifnot(
    isTRUE(all.equal(max(npath_m), 0.089)),
    isTRUE(all.equal(max(ortrue_m), 0.039)),
    isTRUE(all.equal(npath_abw, 0.0009)),
    min(npath_grid) == 250, max(npath_grid) == 2e5,
    misspec_npath$info$reps == 10000)
}
```

```{r}
#| label: n-both-data
#| include: false
# both propensity scores on the sample sizes the two grids share, n = 500 to
# 50k, 10 000 replications per cell on the same draws (stored section
# n_both, handoff/R/sections.R); "both" pools the two specifications' cells
n_both <- read_summary("n_both")
# the captions of tbl-n-adv and tbl-app-n-ref give the grid and the cells,
# which differ between the pooled block and the single-specification ones,
# so stop if the stored ones differ
n_both_k <- n_both$avg |>
  filter(set == "all", theta == "pair", outcome == "pooled") |>
  summarise(k = max(n_cells), .by = block)
stopifnot(identical(sort(unique(n_both$perf$n)),
                    c(500, 1000, 5000, 10000, 50000)),
          all(n_both_k$k[match(c("correct", "misspec", "both"),
                               n_both_k$block)] == c(15, 15, 30)))
# n_both stores more pairs than tbl-n-adv shows
n_adv_pairs <- tribble(
  ~A,              ~B,
  "abw_balnet0",   "balnet0",
  "abw_balnet0",   "aipw_glmnetcv",
  "abw_balnet0",   "glmnetcv_hajek",
  "balnet0",       "aipw_glmnetcv",
  "balnet0",       "glmnetcv_hajek",
  "aipw_glmnetcv", "glmnetcv_hajek"
)
```

We begin with the sample-size grid, under a correctly specified and a misspecified propensity score (@tbl-n-adv). Balancing weights have lower RMSE than MLE weights in every cell under either specification. At exact balance, ABW collapses to the unaugmented `balnet`, and together they average $68.6\%$ lower RMSE than the Hájek estimator and $33.8\%$ lower than AIPW. Pooled across specifications, `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ no longer beats the oracle in every cell, though it still does under quadratic outcomes (@atbl-app-n-ref). Against OLS, the approximation error of its logistic weights pulls in both directions and cancels out on average under a correctly specified score.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-n-adv
#| tbl-cap: "$\\bar R(\\Theta)$ and $\\bar s_m(\\Theta)$ of A against B, $n$ = 500 to 50k."
#| tbl-pos: "!htbp"
#| echo: false
table_avg(n_both, blocks = c("both", "correct", "misspec"),
          pairs = n_adv_pairs, cell_counts = FALSE,
          note = paste("The averages are over 30 cells, 15 per",
                       "specification, at 10 000 Monte Carlo replications."))
```

**Under a correctly specified propensity score,** the balancing estimators have lower RMSE than every modelling estimator across outcome functions, the one exception a near-zero difference against AIPW under linear outcomes. Here, the difference between modelling and balancing is bias driven while balancing's advantage over the oracle comes through variance, consistent with its theoretical efficiency [@wager2024]. Beyond these sample sizes, the correctly specified grid to $n = 400{,}000$ shows the same ordering, with balancing's lead over modelling widening slightly with $n$ (@atbl-q1-adv). AIPW also recovers much of the RMSE losses of the unaugmented modelling weights, less so where the shared outcome model is wrong, under the quadratic and exponential outcomes.

**Under a misspecified propensity score,** both models are fitted on $\tilde X$ and are doubly wrong (@tbl-spec). Both balancing estimators keep substantially lower RMSE in every cell, consistent with the findings of @tan2020a. Their average lead across $n$ runs from $96.9\%$ over the HT estimator at the extreme to $54.3\%$ over AIPW in modelling's best case (@atbl-app-avg-n-m; @tbl-n-adv). The lead of the unaugmented balancing weights over the Hájek estimator is about the same as under a correct score, but its source changes. The unaugmented `balnet` now carries a higher share of bias while the Hájek estimator's error is mostly variance.

Averaging over outcome functions also hides a reversal. Under a correctly specified score, balancing's lead was largest under the linear outcome. Misspecification reverses that ordering. Here the linear outcome is balancing's worst case, misspecification multiplying the RMSE of `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ relative to the Hájek estimator's by $2.4$ and pushing it behind the oracle (@tbl-n-adv; @atbl-app-n-ref). Conversely, it now performs best under the quadratic, where previously its lead over the Hájek estimator was smallest, misspecification dividing the same ratio by $2.4$. Following @benmichael2021, the relative loss of `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ here comes from balancing being unable to improve past exact balance on $\tilde X$. The Hájek estimator may be spared because its errors sit where the score is small, a region the linear outcome keeps moderate [@tan2020a].

For the augmented estimators we take the two cases in turn, the outcome model refitted on the true covariates $X$ and both models fitted on $\tilde X$. The first is a benchmark an analyst who sees only $\tilde X$ cannot reach, and shows the double robustness the augmented estimators provide when the outcome model is correct in both function and covariates.

@fig-n-refit follows the two augmented estimators with the outcome model refitted on $X$ from $n = 250$ to $10^6$ under the linear outcome function, with `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ and the Hájek estimator alongside for reference. The correct outcome model leaves both augmented estimators approximately unbiased beyond the smallest samples, but their RMSE parts as $n$ grows. ABW's falls with $n$ while AIPW's turns upward alongside the Hájek estimator's, whose weights it shares. The gap is the cost of the wrong weights, which a correct outcome model strips of bias but not variance [@benmichael2021]. Across $n$ this leaves ABW $52\%$ below AIPW under the linear outcome and about three quarters lower when the outcome function is also misspecified (@atbl-app-avg-n-m).

```{r}
#| label: fig-n-refit
#| fig-cap: "Outcome model refitted on $X$ by $n$, misspecified propensity score, linear outcome. $n$ = 1M (dotted) is a separate run."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.0
#| eval: !expr npath_built
#| include: !expr npath_built
#| echo: false
fig_npath_strips(misspec_npath, ortrue_arms, outcomes = "linear",
                 measures = npath_measures, separate = 1e6,
                 title = expression(paste("Outcome model refitted on ", italic(X))))
```

Once both models are fitted on the observed $\tilde X$, the double fragility of AIPW is clear. The outcome model that protected it in the refit is now a second source of error. Fitted on $\tilde X$, it leaves the part of the outcome missed by its linear covariates in its residuals, which are then weighted by the misspecified MLE weights, so the bias is the imbalance those weights leave in the residual [@benmichael2021].

@fig-n-misspec follows `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ and the modelling estimators across our three doubly wrong settings. Our balancing estimator converges, but to the wrong value, as is expected of a misspecified estimator. Its variance shrinks towards zero and its bias settles near $-0.22$, $-0.07$ and $-0.14$ under the linear, quadratic and exponential outcome functions (@atbl-n-path). We focus on the Hájek and AIPW estimators, as the poor performance of the HT estimator is well documented [@kang2007; @busso2014], and leave its results to the appendix.

```{r}
#| label: fig-n-misspec
#| fig-cap: "Both models fitted on $\\tilde X$ by $n$, misspecified propensity score. $n$ = 1M (dotted) is a separate run. ABW coincides with balnet from $n$ = 500."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 6.0
#| eval: !expr npath_built
#| include: !expr npath_built
#| echo: false
fig_npath_strips(misspec_npath, npath_arms, measures = npath_measures,
                 separate = 1e6,
                 title = expression(paste("Both models fitted on ", tilde(italic(X)))))
```

The Hájek estimator does not settle. Under every outcome function its bias shrinks through zero and then grows positive, and its RMSE passes a minimum and rises to the largest sample. More data makes it worse, a direction @testa2026 also saw to $n = 1000$. @kang2007 traced the worsening to a few enormous weights where the fitted model misses in the region of near-zero scores. As $n$ grows those tails lengthen rather than settling, and the share of the sample carrying the weight shrinks with it. At $n = 500$ the MLE weights are no more extreme than the true score's, with a similar largest weight and a larger effective sample size (@atbl-app-n-diag-m-lin), so the tails cannot explain the bias. Here, the bias comes from the imbalance the weights leave in $\tilde X$.

Under the linear outcome function the balancing weights settle at the same bias alone and augmented, near $-0.2$, well below the Hájek estimator. Augmented, they reduce to OLS on $\tilde X$, as exact balance makes the outcome model a linear adjustment on $\tilde X$ [@brunssmith2025]. Unaugmented, they differ from that OLS only by the approximation error, so both carry the part of the outcome not linear in $\tilde X$. The double fragility of AIPW is pronounced here. Its path starts ahead of the Hájek estimator, slips behind it by $n = 2000$, and loses ground from there to over three times its RMSE by $n = 10^6$ (@atbl-n-path). This is the ordering @kang2007 report up to $n = 1000$, here holding to $10^6$. For AIPW, two wrong models have previously been found to beat one when the outcome model's misspecification is moderate, though every bias still scales with the propensity score error [@warp2023]. Here the two errors compound instead.

Under the quadratic and exponential outcome functions the outcome model is also wrong in form, yet AIPW now beats the Hájek estimator, likely because the linear model in $\tilde X$ picks up part of the outcome's curvature, so its residual is less imbalanced than the outcome itself [@benmichael2021]. It still stays well behind ABW, and `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ pulls further ahead of the Hájek estimator. Under the exponential, AIPW is the one modelling series that settles, at a bias near $-0.13$. The outcome's $\exp(X_1/2)$ term is linear in $\tilde X_1$, so the outcome model may fit exactly the part of the outcome where most of the score's signal sits. Refitting the outcome model on $X$ does not rescue AIPW under either outcome function, and under the quadratic it makes both augmented estimators worse at large $n$. The same wrong-form model costs almost nothing under a correctly specified propensity score, where both augmented estimators are nearly unbiased, so what AIPW appears unable to carry is the pairing of two wrong models.

Misspecification costs the balancing weights a fixed bias that more data does not shrink. For modelling, it costs the weights a bias that falls, crosses zero and grows again while their tails lengthen with $n$, and that bias compounds in AIPW under the linear outcome function. Balancing stays ahead at every $n$ under every outcome function, alone and augmented, and the bias of `cv.glmnet` has not settled by $n = 10^6$.

## Overlap {#sec-s1-overlap}

```{r}
#| label: adv-ov
#| include: false
# overlap7 (n = 1000) and overlap8 (n = 10 000), c = 0.05 to 2, 10 000 reps
# (runs/aipw/aipw_overlap.R, runs/aipw/aipw_overlap10k_dgp2.R), both
# specifications on the same draws; each summary averages over every (n, c)
# cell, and "Both specifications" pools both specifications' cells. Sets of
# c (poor: c <= 0.25, good: c >= 0.5) are in handoff/R/sections.R
overlap <- read_summary("overlap")
# the rows the text reads from each table: over all c pooled over both
# specifications, and by specification for the good and poor sets
ov_rows <- list(
  all = tribble(
    ~block,    ~A,            ~B,
    "both",    "balnet0",     "aipw_glmnetcv",
    "both",    "balnet0",     "glmnetcv_hajek",
    "both",    "abw_balnet0", "balnet0",
    "both",    "abw_balnet0", "aipw_glmnetcv"),
  good = tribble(
    ~block,    ~A,            ~B,
    "correct", "balnet0",     "aipw_glmnetcv",
    "correct", "abw_balnet0", "balnet0",
    "correct", "abw_balnet0", "aipw_glmnetcv",
    "misspec", "balnet0",     "aipw_glmnetcv",
    "misspec", "abw_balnet0", "aipw_glmnetcv"),
  poor = tribble(
    ~block,    ~A,            ~B,
    "correct", "balnet0",     "aipw_glmnetcv",
    "correct", "abw_balnet0", "aipw_glmnetcv",
    "misspec", "balnet0",     "aipw_glmnetcv",
    "misspec", "abw_balnet0", "aipw_glmnetcv")
)
ov_shown <- map(ov_rows, \(rows) {
  s <- overlap
  s$avg <- semi_join(overlap$avg, rows, by = c("block", "A", "B"))
  s
})
```

Pooled over overlap and both specifications, balancing estimators have lower RMSE on average, and `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ has lower RMSE than the Hájek estimator in every cell (@tbl-ov-adv). ABW has on average $20.2\%$ lower RMSE than `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ and $32.5\%$ lower than AIPW, while the unaugmented `balnet` has on average $23.1\%$ lower than AIPW and $59.9\%$ lower than the Hájek estimator.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ov-adv
#| tbl-cap: "$\\bar R(\\Theta)$ and $\\bar s_m(\\Theta)$ of A against B, $c$ = 0.05 to 2, $n$ = 1000 and 10 000, both specifications."
#| tbl-pos: "!htbp"
#| echo: false
table_avg(ov_shown$all, cell_counts = FALSE,
          note = paste("The averages are over 84 cells, 42 per",
                       "specification, at 10 000 Monte Carlo replications.",
                       "Pairs with glmnet omit the six correct-specification",
                       "cells at $c$ = 0.05, where glmnet lacks more than 1%",
                       "of its estimates."))
```

AIPW has lower RMSE than `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ on average only where common support is practically violated and the propensity score is correctly specified. There MLE's performance is also unobservable at $c = 0.05$, where $81.8\%$ of the sample have a propensity score below $0.01$ or above $0.99$ (@atbl-ov-levels).

Where we assume common support holds, both balancing estimators have lower RMSE on average than the modelling estimators, with ABW averaging $7.5\%$ lower RMSE than AIPW and $0.2\%$ lower than `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ across outcome functions (@tbl-ov-adv-hi). Balancing's advantage here holds across nonlinear outcomes, though for the linear outcome function, where the shared outcome model is correct, ABW has $0.6\%$ higher RMSE than AIPW while `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ has $0.8\%$ higher. For misspecified propensity scores, both balancing estimators have RMSE around $51\%$ lower than AIPW, as on the sample-size grid.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ov-adv-hi
#| tbl-cap: "$\\bar R(\\Theta)$ and $\\bar s_m(\\Theta)$ of A against B where common support holds."
#| tbl-pos: "!htbp"
#| echo: false
table_avg(ov_shown$good, set = "good", cell_counts = FALSE,
          note = paste("Overlap $c$ = 0.5 to 2 at $n$ = 1000 and 10 000. The",
                       "averages are over 24 cells per specification, at",
                       "10 000 Monte Carlo replications."))
```

Where we assume common support is violated, under a correctly specified score ABW has $21.7\%$ lower RMSE than AIPW while the unaugmented `balnet` has around $1.5$ times the RMSE of AIPW (@tbl-ov-adv-lo). This ordering holds under every outcome function, with the gap to `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ widest under the linear outcome. Under a misspecified score, for all $c \leq 0.25$ ABW has $37.7\%$ lower RMSE than AIPW on average, while `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ has $29.3\%$ lower. As in simulations with practical or outright positivity violations, `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ has lower RMSE than the Hájek estimator [@chattopadhyay2020; @keele2025] but is biased where its path truncates. Under a misspecified score the lowest RMSE at the weakest overlap does not improve with $n$ (@atbl-app-ov-full-m).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ov-adv-lo
#| tbl-cap: "$\\bar R(\\Theta)$ and $\\bar s_m(\\Theta)$ of A against B where common support is violated."
#| tbl-pos: "!htbp"
#| echo: false
table_avg(ov_shown$poor, set = "poor", cell_counts = FALSE,
          note = paste("Overlap $c$ = 0.05 to 0.25 at $n$ = 1000 and 10 000.",
                       "The averages are over 12 cells under correct",
                       "specification and 18 under misspecification, at",
                       "10 000 Monte Carlo replications."))
```

```{r}
#| label: adv-ov-share
#| include: false
# share of bias per arm, c and outcome, averaged over n = 1000 and 10 000
# (set by_c in handoff/R/sections.R); grey where an arm lacks any n at that c
ov_cbar <- heat_share_avg(overlap, set = "by_c", x = "overlap",
                          arms = text_arms,
                          x_lab = expression("Overlap " * italic(c)),
                          x_fmt = fmt_dot)
ov_cbar_share <- ov_cbar$share
# of the chart's note, only the grey-cell sentence, when there is one
ov_cbar_note <- regmatches(ov_cbar$note, regexpr("Grey cells[^.]*\\.", ov_cbar$note))
ov_cbar_height <- ov_cbar$height
```

As overlap degrades below $c = 0.5$, the share of bias rises for both balancing estimators. Under correct specification, averaged over both sample sizes, the unaugmented `balnet` jumps from a $1\%$ share at $c = 0.5$ to $41\%$ at $c = 0.25$ under linear outcomes (@fig-ov-adv). This average hides a split by sample size, with the share $83\%$ at $n = 1000$, where every path stops short, and zero at $n = 10{,}000$, where nearly every path reaches its target (@atbl-app-ov-full-c). In contrast, ABW moves from unbiased to a $6\%$ share, rising to $28\%$ by $c = 0.05$ where `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ is at $97\%$. This pattern holds across outcomes, except that ABW under quadratic outcomes becomes more variance driven on either side of $c = 0.25$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ov-adv
#| fig-cap: !expr paste("Share of bias by $c$, averaged over $n$ = 1000 and 10 000, both specifications. glmnet (HT) not drawn.", ov_cbar_note)
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: !expr ov_cbar_height
#| echo: false
ov_cbar_share
```

```{r}
#| label: ov-nc-data
#| include: false
# DGP2, p = 50, n x c grid (12 n x 13 c), both PS specifications, seed 202,
# 1000 reps, same draws (runs/aipw/aipw_n_by_overlap_dgp2.R); stored
# summary "nc": every arm and cell, and the share of truncated paths
nc <- read_summary("nc")
nc_fig_n <- c(200, 5000)
# afig-app-nc's caption is typed in Appendix D; the render stops here if
# the stored numbers no longer match it
nc_m <- signif(nc_mcse(nc, nc_fig_n), 2)
nc_left_out <- filter(nc$perf, n %in% nc_fig_n, dropped)
stopifnot(
  nc$info$reps == 1000,
  max(nc_m) == 0.23, nc_m[["glmnetcv_hajek"]] == 0.23,
  all(nc_left_out$spec == "correct"))
```

@afig-app-nc follows the estimators as overlap improves in small and large samples. Across all settings, ABW has lower RMSE than the unaugmented `balnet` wherever the path of `balnet` stops short of exact balance, increasingly so under a correctly specified score as overlap degrades, and with more data the path reaches exact balance at poorer overlap.

Where we assume common support holds, ABW has the lowest RMSE of the modelling and balancing estimators in small samples under every outcome. In these samples AIPW also has a lower RMSE than `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ under a correctly specified score, and this extends to larger samples as overlap degrades. Under a misspecified propensity score the advantage of `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ over AIPW extends to poorer overlap, with a lower RMSE at $n = 5000$ from $c = 0.1$, even where its path truncates, and at every $c$ under linear outcomes.

Where we assume common support is practically violated, `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ truncates at every $n$, with a higher RMSE than ABW in both samples, far more so under a correctly specified score. Under a misspecified score AIPW has a lower RMSE than ABW at the weakest overlap under the quadratic outcome and the two are level under the exponential, but as overlap improves ABW takes over, earlier in the larger sample, consistent with approximate residual balancing outperforming AIPW in the misspecified setting of @athey2018, which varied dimension. At the weakest overlap no weighting estimator removes half the confounding in either sample, as in @keele2025, where no method overcame outcome misspecification once overlap was poor.[^6]

[^6]: At $c = 0.01$ the unadjusted difference is $-2.06$ (linear, quadratic) and $-1.56$ (exponential) at both $n$, against a lowest weighting RMSE of $1.08$ (design values, weighting RMSEs in @atbl-app-nc-full-m).

## High-dimensional settings {#sec-s1-hd}

```{r}
#| label: adv-p
#| include: false
# p/n = 0.05 to 4 at n = 500 and 1000, s = 4, both specifications on the
# same draws (runs/aipw/aipw_paxis_dgp2.R)
p_axis <- read_summary("p_axis")
p_heat <- heat_cells(p_axis, x = "pn", by = "n", arms = text_arms,
                     x_lab = expression(italic(p) / italic(n)),
                     x_fmt = fmt_dot)
```

```{r}
#| label: pn-data
#| include: false
# the shares of balnet paths that stop short, stored with the appendix entry
# (app_p_axis), place the shading of the p/n figures; the pairs are the ones
# the text quotes
app_p_axis <- read_summary("app_p_axis")
pn_pairs <- tribble(
  ~A,            ~B,
  "balnet0",     "glmnetcv_hajek",
  "balnet0",     "aipw_glmnetcv",
  "abw_balnet0", "balnet0",
  "abw_balnet0", "aipw_glmnetcv"
)
# the captions of fig-pn-rmse and afig-app-pn-bias are typed, so the render
# stops here if the stored numbers no longer match them
pn_rmse_m <- signif(pn_lines_mcse(p_axis, "rmse"), 2)
pn_bias_m <- signif(pn_lines_mcse(p_axis, "bias"), 2)
pn_trunc <- pn_trunc_share(app_p_axis)
stopifnot(
  pn_rmse_m[["glmnetcv_hajek"]] == 0.053,
  max(pn_rmse_m[names(pn_rmse_m) != "glmnetcv_hajek"]) == 0.016,
  max(pn_bias_m) == 0.0051,
  all(pn_trunc$share[pn_trunc$pn >= 0.5] == 1),
  max(pn_trunc$share[pn_trunc$pn < 0.5]) < 0.06,
  p_axis$info$reps == 10000)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pn-adv
#| tbl-cap: "$\\bar R(\\Theta)$ of A against B and $\\bar s_m(\\Theta)$ of A over all $p/n$, at exact balance and once the path stops short, $n$ = 500 and 1000."
#| tbl-pos: "!htbp"
#| echo: false
table_pn_regimes(p_axis, pn_pairs)
```

As covariates are added, balancing keeps its advantage over modelling on average, alone and augmented (@tbl-pn-adv). `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ has lower RMSE than `cv.glmnet` (Hájek) in every cell, by $49.1\%$ on average under a correctly specified score and $39.2\%$ under misspecification. Augmentation narrows this to $13.6\%$ and $17.8\%$ for ABW over AIPW, and on average AIPW overtakes the unaugmented `balnet`.

These averages hide the expected change at $p/n = 0.5$, from which every `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ path stops short of exact balance. Bias then makes up most of its error, with its share rising from $0.01$ to $0.89$ under a correctly specified score (@tbl-pn-adv). Here, its lead over the Hájek estimator nearly halves, from $66.9\%$ to $36.9\%$, and it also slips behind the oracle (@atbl-app-pn-full-c).

ABW again collapses to `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ at exact balance. Once the path stops short, the outcome model adjusts for the remaining imbalance, and ABW's RMSE is $55.4\%$ and $33.5\%$ lower than that of `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$. Unlike `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$, ABW stays ahead of AIPW, by $18.4\%$ and $13.7\%$. Its lead widens from $p/n = 0.5$ under a correctly specified score but narrows under misspecification.

Once the path stops short, the lead of `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ over the Hájek estimator narrows as $p$ grows under all settings (@fig-pn-rmse). Both estimators grow more biased, but at different rates. As expected, the bias of the Hájek estimator grows gradually, while that of `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ grows faster as its leftover imbalance increases with $p$ [@zhao2019]. Its nonzero coefficients stop growing with $p$ once the path stops short (@atbl-app-pn-diag-c-lin; @atbl-app-pn-diag-m-lin). Our grid extends the comparison of @tan2020a to higher dimensions, up to $p/n = 4$, where the narrowing we find between the unaugmented estimators mirrors the result of @athey2018 for approximately balancing weights.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pn-rmse
#| fig-cap: "RMSE against $p/n$ at $n$ = 500 and 1000, both specifications. Shading marks where the balnet path stops short, the dotted line $p = n$."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| echo: false
pn_lines(p_axis, app_p_axis, "rmse",
         title = expression(paste("RMSE against ", italic(p) / italic(n))))
```

Augmentation does not remove the whole cost of the leftover imbalance, with ABW's bias still growing with $p$ from $p/n = 0.5$ (@afig-app-pn-bias). Its lead over AIPW holds steady at $15\%$ to $21\%$ under a correctly specified score (@atbl-app-pn-full-c), but narrows as $p$ grows under misspecification, most clearly for the linear outcome. The narrowing comes from both sides, as ABW's bias grows faster than AIPW's once the path stops short, while AIPW's variance falls with $p$ and offsets its own growing bias, most of all at $n = 1000$. To our knowledge this narrowing has not been reported, and the augmented balancing weights of @athey2018, which target balance without a propensity score, show a steady lead over AIPW.[^7]

[^7]: Unlike ours, their AIPW used elastic-net propensity scores trimmed at 0.05 and 0.95 [@athey2018].

The cost of misspecification to the MLE estimators shrinks as covariates are added. For the Hájek estimator this cost falls in every series, and has vanished or reversed for nonlinear outcomes by $p/n = 4$. Though the relative cost falls, Hájek's RMSE still generally rises with $p$, consistent with the findings of @athey2018. As discussed earlier, misspecification costs AIPW more than the Hájek estimator at low $p$, and this cost too shrinks as $p$ grows (@fig-pn-rmse).

```{r}
#| label: adv-sp
#| include: false
# n x p/n x s x decay x covariance structure, correct specification, linear
# and quadratic outcomes (runs/aipw/sparsity_axis.R: iid and AR(1) in one
# grid, equicorrelated in its own); structures and nu as in the DGM section
sparsity <- read_summary("sparsity")
# the regimes are kept apart, each in the same order (sets in
# handoff/R/sections.R; s = 64 is not run at n = 500, p/n = 0.1). The
# truncated sets by covariance structure also store rows by decay, which
# the text does not use, so only their rows by s are shown, as at exact
# balance
sp_sets <- sparsity
sp_sets$avg <- filter(sp_sets$avg,
                      !(set %in% c("truncated_iid", "truncated_ar1",
                                   "truncated_equi") & factor %in% "decay"))
sp_factor_labs <- c(s = "confounders s", decay = "decay ν",
                    corr = "covariates")
# RMSE of each estimator against s, pooled over the cells of the tables in
# Appendix F (fig_sp_change() stops if the two disagree)
sp_change <- fig_sp_change(sparsity)
```

**With a denser covariate profile:** With four confounders, $\nu = 1$ and independent covariates, the sparsity grid shares the propensity score of the $p/n$ grid. From $p/n = 0.5$ every `balnet` path stops short of exact balance, whatever $s$, $\nu$ or $\rho$, so exact balance and the truncated path are reported apart throughout (@fig-sp-change). `balnet` again has lower RMSE than the Hájek estimator in every cell under both scores, and by more than three MCSE in all but one under Tan's transformation, whatever the number of confounders, their decay or the covariate correlation.[^8] ABW keeps a lead over AIPW on average under independent and AR(1)-correlated covariates, but under equicorrelation the two stay within a few per cent.

[^8]: In the remaining cell ($n = 1000$, $s = 4$, $\nu = 1$, AR(1), quadratic outcome) the RMSE of `balnet` is $40\%$ of the Hájek estimator's, but heavy-tailed Hájek estimates leave the ratio within three MCSE of one, so it is not counted as a win.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sp-change
#| fig-cap: "RMSE by $s$ and covariance structure, correct specification, at exact balance and once the path stops short, pooled over outcomes and decay rates. glmnet (HT) not drawn."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: !expr sp_change$height
#| echo: false
sp_change$plot
```

**Dynamics across** $s$: While exact balance holds, `balnet` stays close to unbiased in every cell, with absolute bias at most 0.006 for the linear outcome and 0.028 for the quadratic, at every $s$, $\nu$ and $\rho$ (@atbl-app-sp-cells). Here, the Hájek estimator grows more biased as confounders are added under independent and AR(1)-correlated covariates, so the lead of `balnet` widens with $s$, from $62.2\%$ to $71.1\%$ under independent and from $56.5\%$ to $65.3\%$ under AR(1)-correlated covariates at $n = 1000$. The lead is larger under slower decay, whereas under equicorrelation it narrows instead (@atbl-app-sp-exact). As expected, the error of the MLE weights grows with the number of active covariates [@tan2020b]. Exact balance instead removes the bias for the linear outcome at any $s$.

Once the path stops short, all four estimators are biased downwards (@atbl-app-sp-cells). The bias of `balnet` grows as confounders are added and, beyond four, as their decay slows, and is smaller under AR(1)-correlated covariates, consistent with the findings of @zhao2019 for the number of confounders and of @athey2018 for correlation. Under equicorrelation it falls with $s$ instead. `balnet` still keeps a lead of $37\%$ to $48\%$ over the Hájek estimator at every $s$, though its error turns to bias, with a share rising from 0.73 to 0.86 under independent and from 0.60 to 0.76 under AR(1)-correlated covariates (@atbl-app-sp-trunc). Its linear bias is nearly the full imbalance bound with four confounders but between a half and three quarters of it with 64 under independent and AR(1)-correlated covariates (@atbl-app-sp-bound).

The gain from augmentation follows the same split. Once the path stops short, ABW has lower RMSE than AIPW in every cell under independent and AR(1)-correlated covariates, and its lead grows with $s$, from $20.1\%$ to $28\%$ by 16 confounders under independent and from $10.0\%$ to $32.5\%$ under AR(1)-correlated covariates (@atbl-app-sp-trunc). Under these two structures both augmented estimators grow more biased as confounders are added, AIPW faster. As expected, AIPW loses ground as the propensity model it relies on grows denser [@athey2018]. This is consistent with the findings of @bradic2019, where the error of AIPW rose with the number of active propensity covariates while that of augmented balancing weights did not. While exact balance holds, the same pattern appears at $n = 1000$, from a lead of $5.8\%$ under independent and none under AR(1)-correlated covariates at four confounders to $35.0\%$ and $12.5\%$ at 64.

The unaugmented `balnet` also catches AIPW as confounders are added. Once the path stops short, `balnet` has 1.3 times the RMSE of AIPW at four confounders under independent and AR(1)-correlated covariates. At 64 it is level with AIPW under AR(1)-correlated covariates and ahead under independent ones, and the gap shrinks with $s$ under every covariance structure (@atbl-app-sp-trunc). Here, the bias of AIPW grows with $s$ faster than that of `balnet`, while under equicorrelation the bias of `balnet` falls faster.

Tan's transformation costs `balnet`, not the Hájek estimator, and only while exact balance holds. There the RMSE of `balnet` rises by about a half under independent covariates, two thirds for the linear outcome, and by a fifth under AR(1), so the lead narrows from $63.6\%$ to $49.6\%$ under independent covariates and little elsewhere (@atbl-app-sp-tan). Here, exact balance on the transformed covariates does not guarantee balance in the original ones, in which the outcome is linear, so part of the confounding bias can return [@zhao2019]. This differs from the findings of @tan2020a, where balancing weights had similar or smaller MSE under a correct score and a substantial advantage under a Kang–Schafer misspecification. Under the transformation the lead of ABW over AIPW also narrows with $s$ at exact balance, the reverse of its direction under a correct score. The direction matches the findings of @tan2020b under a misspecified score, though their outcome model was correct.

Equicorrelated covariates break the pattern. While exact balance holds, the Hájek estimator grows less biased as confounders are added, so the lead of `balnet` narrows from $47.7\%$ to $40.4\%$ instead of widening, and once the path stops short the bias of `balnet` falls with $s$ too (@atbl-app-sp-exact; @atbl-app-sp-trunc). ABW and AIPW stay within a few per cent of each other at exact balance and once the path stops short, and Tan's transformation costs `balnet` little. We read this through $Z_0$, the common factor every equicorrelated covariate shares, which makes up about three quarters of the variance of the propensity index at four confounders and over nine tenths at 64 (@atbl-app-sp-share). Here, a sparse fit already captures most of the confounding, so balancing more columns adds little.

## Outcome signal {#sec-s1-signal}

```{r}
#| label: adv-sig
#| include: false
# outcome signal strength 0.02 to 1 at n = 1000, p = 50, both
# specifications on the same draws (runs/aipw/aipw_strength.R)
signal <- read_summary("signal")
sig_heat <- heat_cells(signal, x = "strength", arms = text_arms,
                       x_fmt = fmt_dot,
                       x_lab = expression("Outcome signal strength " * kappa))
```

Under a correctly specified propensity score, the ranking of `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ and the Hájek estimator reverses as the outcome signal grows against the fixed noise (@atbl-app-sig-full-c). As only the ratio of signal to noise decides the ranking, a low $\kappa$ reads as a noisy outcome. In the noisiest cells, $\kappa \le 0.05$, `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ has $9\%$ to $12\%$ higher RMSE, and once the noise falls back, from $\kappa = 0.2$, it has lower RMSE, by $62\%$ to $74\%$ at $\kappa = 1$. Here, the bias of the Hájek estimator grows with the signal while `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ stays close to unbiased, but exact balance leaves it a smaller effective sample size (median 345 against 430 per arm, @atbl-app-sig-diag-c-lin), which decides the ranking while the noise dominates. Its $32.9\%$ advantage pooled over $\kappa$ (@tbl-sig-adv) averages over the cells where its RMSE is higher. The oracle reverses against `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ in the same way, so the efficiency advantage of exact balance holds only once the signal clears the noise.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sig-adv
#| tbl-cap: "$\\bar R(\\Theta)$ and $\\bar s_m(\\Theta)$ of balnet against glmnet (Hájek), correct specification, $\\kappa$ = 0.02 to 1."
#| tbl-pos: "!htbp"
#| echo: false
# the comparison the text quotes from this table
table_avg(signal, blocks = "correct",
          pairs = tibble(A = "balnet0", B = "glmnetcv_hajek"),
          cell_counts = FALSE,
          note = paste("The averages are over 24 cells at 10 000 Monte Carlo",
                       "replications."))
```

Under a misspecified propensity score both estimators are biased in proportion to the signal, as the bias acts through the outcome [@zhao2019; @warp2023], but the Hájek estimator is about twice as biased. `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ has lower RMSE at every noise level but the highest, by $49\%$ to $68\%$ at $\kappa = 1$, and the two are level at $\kappa = 0.02$. There the Hájek estimator has the lower median absolute error, as a few extreme weights lift its RMSE.

Augmentation again leaves `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ unchanged, with the RMSE of ABW within 0.001 of it in every cell. Under a correctly specified score the gain for the Hájek estimator grows as the noise falls, from none at $\kappa = 0.02$, where the outcome model often keeps no covariate, to $59\%$ to $74\%$ lower RMSE at $\kappa = 1$. The augmented pair reverses as the unaugmented one does, with ABW ahead of AIPW only from $\kappa = 0.2$, by under $8\%$. Under misspecification neither pair reverses, and ABW stays ahead of AIPW at every noise level but the highest, by $18\%$ to $43\%$ at $\kappa = 1$.

In a noisy outcome, then, the balance at the end of the `balnet` path costs more in variance than it removes in bias, as anticipated where the best amount of balance depends on the noise relative to the signal [@zhao2019].

## Coverage {#sec-s1-coverage}

```{r}
#| label: cov-data
#| include: false
# Coverage at the empirical SE (Performance measures): the share of
# replications with |tau_hat_r| <= 1.96 EmpSE, tau = 0, per cell, with its
# binomial MCSE. Built once from results/aipw through handoff's reader
# (handoff/R/build.R, read_results()) and stored in
# output/thesis_summaries/coverage_empse.rds; delete that file to rebuild.
# Grids: n (correct n = 500 to 400k; misspecified n = 500 to 50k and the
# separate n = 1M run), overlap (c = 0.05 to 2 at n = 1000 and 10 000) and
# outcome signal (kappa = 0.02 to 1 at n = 1000), both specifications, the four estimators the text follows and Oracle
# (Hájek) as the unbiased reference
cov_path <- here::here("output", "thesis_summaries", "coverage_empse.rds")
cov_arms <- c(text_arms, "oracle_hajek")
cov_grids <- c("n", "overlap", "signal", "diag")
if (!file.exists(cov_path) ||
    !all(cov_grids %in% names(readRDS(cov_path)))) {
  build_env <- new.env()
  sys.source(here::here("handoff", "R", "build.R"), envir = build_env)
  z <- qnorm(0.975)
  cov_cells <- function(long, spec) {
    long |>
      filter(is.finite(error)) |>
      group_by(across(-c(level, sim, error))) |>
      summarise(m = n(), bias = mean(error), empse = sd(error),
                coverage = mean(abs(error) <= z * empse), .groups = "drop") |>
      mutate(mcse = sqrt(coverage * (1 - coverage) / m), spec = spec)
  }
  cov_files <- list(
    n = list(
      correct = "aipw_correct_n400k_dgp2.csv.gz",
      misspec = c("aipw_misspec_n_dgp2.csv.gz", "aipw_misspec_n_dgp2n1mill.csv.gz")),
    overlap = list(
      correct = c("aipw_correct_overlap7_dgp2.csv.gz", "aipw_correct_overlap8_dgp2.csv.gz"),
      misspec = c("aipw_misspec_overlap7_dgp2.csv.gz", "aipw_misspec_overlap8_dgp2.csv.gz")),
    signal = list(
      correct = "aipw_correct_strength_dgp2.csv.gz",
      misspec = "aipw_misspec_strength_dgp2.csv.gz"))
  coverage_empse <- imap(cov_files, \(specs, grid) {
    imap(specs, \(fs, spec) {
      map(fs, \(f) build_env$read_results(f, cov_arms)) |>
        bind_rows() |>
        cov_cells(spec)
    }) |> bind_rows()
  })
  # the MLE weights by overlap level, behind the Hájek estimator's loss of
  # coverage at c = 2 (footnote cov-wmax): median largest weight and
  # effective sample size of the treated arm, by specification and n
  coverage_empse$diag <- imap(cov_files$overlap, \(fs, spec) {
    map(fs, \(f) build_env$read_results(f, c("wmax_glm1", "ess_glm1"))) |>
      bind_rows() |>
      filter(outcome == "linear", is.finite(error)) |>
      summarise(value = median(error), .by = c(n, overlap, estimator)) |>
      mutate(spec = spec)
  }) |> bind_rows()
  saveRDS(coverage_empse, cov_path)
  write.csv(bind_rows(coverage_empse, .id = "grid"),
            sub("rds$", "csv", cov_path), row.names = FALSE)
}
coverage_empse <- readRDS(cov_path)
cov_m <- signif(max(map_dbl(coverage_empse[cov_grids != "diag"],
                            \(d) max(d$mcse))), 1)
# the typed numbers of the section (footnote cov-wmax, the n and signal
# paragraphs): the render stops here if the stored files no longer give them
cov_wm <- \(est, c) coverage_empse$diag |>
  filter(spec == "misspec", n == 1e4, overlap == c, estimator == est) |>
  pull(value)
cov_hj <- coverage_empse$overlap |>
  filter(spec == "misspec", n == 1e4, overlap == 2, outcome == "linear",
         estimator == "glmnetcv_hajek")
cov_sg <- \(oc) coverage_empse$signal |>
  filter(spec == "misspec", strength == 1, outcome == oc,
         estimator == "glmnetcv_hajek")
stopifnot(
  round(cov_wm("wmax_glm1", 2)) == 15, round(cov_wm("wmax_glm1", 1)) == 98,
  round(cov_wm("wmax_glm1", 0.05), -1) == 1450,
  round(cov_wm("ess_glm1", 2), -2) == 4600,
  round(cov_hj$empse, 2) == 0.03, round(cov_hj$bias, 2) == -0.15,
  round(cov_sg("quad1")$empse / cov_sg("linear")$empse) == 3,
  abs(cov_sg("quad1")$bias) < abs(cov_sg("linear")$bias),
  max(filter(coverage_empse$n, spec == "correct",
             estimator == "glmnetcv_hajek")$coverage) < 0.445)
# one palette and shape set for both coverage figures: the n-path figures'
# colours for the four estimators, plus the oracle
cov_pal <- c(npath_strip_pal[text_arms], oracle_hajek = "#D55E00")
cov_shape <- c(npath_strip_shape[text_arms], oracle_hajek = 4)
names(cov_pal) <- names(cov_shape) <- arm_labs[cov_arms]
cov_rows <- function(d) {
  d |>
    mutate(estimator = factor(estimator, cov_arms, arm_labs[cov_arms]),
           outcome = factor(outcome, outcome_models, outcome_labs),
           spec = factor(spec, c("correct", "misspec"),
                         block_labs[c("correct", "misspec")]),
           lo = pmax(coverage - 1.96 * mcse, 0),
           hi = pmin(coverage + 1.96 * mcse, 1))
}
cov_theme <- function() {
  list(theme_bw(base_size = 9, base_family = "serif"),
       theme(legend.position = "bottom", strip.background = element_blank(),
             legend.text = element_text(size = 7.5),
             panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
             panel.grid.major = element_line(linewidth = 0.2)),
       guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 1.8))))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-n-coverage
#| fig-cap: "Coverage at the empirical SE by $n$, both specifications. The dotted line is the nominal 95%, $n$ = 1M (misspecified) a separate run."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| echo: false
cov_n <- cov_rows(coverage_empse$n) |>
  mutate(run = if_else(n >= 1e6, "separate", "grid"))
cov_breaks <- c(500, 5e3, 5e4, 5e5)
ggplot(cov_n, aes(n, coverage, colour = estimator, shape = estimator,
                  group = estimator)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.95, linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), linewidth = 0.4, alpha = 0.6,
                 show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_line(data = \(d) filter(d, run == "grid"), linewidth = 0.5,
            show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(size = 1.2) +
  facet_grid(spec ~ outcome) +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = cov_breaks, labels = format_kM(cov_breaks)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), breaks = c(0, 0.5, 0.95)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = cov_pal) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = cov_shape) +
  labs(x = expression(italic(n)), y = "Coverage at the empirical SE",
       colour = NULL, shape = NULL) +
  cov_theme()
```

@fig-n-coverage shows what the biases of Study 1 cost a confidence interval along $n$. Under a correctly specified score `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$, ABW and the oracle sit at nominal at every $n$, and AIPW reaches it by $n = 10{,}000$. The Hájek estimator never rises above $0.44$, as the shrinkage bias of its cross-validated lasso score does not fall with $n$ while its sampling error does (share of bias $0.88$, @tbl-n-adv). Under misspecification the picture inverts. The balancing estimators collapse to zero by $n = 10{,}000$ for the linear and exponential outcomes and more slowly for the quadratic, as the intervals zero in on their fixed bias. The Hájek and AIPW estimators instead reach nominal from $n = 5000$, AIPW from $10{,}000$ under the exponential outcome. In our design the largest MLE weight grows with $n$ while the true score's does not, from a median under ten at $n = 500$ to several hundred at $50{,}000$ (@atbl-app-n-diag-m-lin), so the Hájek and AIPW estimates carry heavy tails that inflate EmpSE beyond the spread of a typical estimate.

Along overlap, coverage depends on the balance achieved (@afig-ov-coverage). Under a correctly specified score `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ holds nominal coverage where common support holds and loses it where it is practically violated, AIPW loses it only at $c \le 0.15$ under the linear and exponential outcomes, and ABW stays at or above $0.83$ at every $c$. The Hájek estimator sits below a half at every $c \ge 0.75$, and at $c = 0.05$ even the oracle falls below $0.15$. Under misspecification the balancing estimators keep partial coverage at $n = 1000$, rising with overlap from near zero at $c \le 0.15$ to between $0.7$ and $0.9$ at $c = 2$, before the collapse with $n$ seen above. The Hájek and AIPW estimators reach nominal only mid-grid and lose it at both ends, under practical violations and at $c = 2$, where the weights are no longer extreme and their bias is exposed.[^9]

[^9]: Under misspecification at $n = 10{,}000$ the largest MLE weight in the treated arm has a median of $15$ at $c = 2$, against $98$ at $c = 1$ and about $1450$ at $c = 0.05$, and the arm's effective sample size is about $4600$ of $5000$. EmpSE of the Hájek estimator falls to $0.03$ while its bias stays near $-0.15$ for the linear outcome.

Noise also obscures bias (@afig-sig-coverage). At low $\kappa$ the noise dominates EmpSE and every estimator reaches nominal coverage. A stronger outcome signal lowers the coverage of a biased estimator, as its bias grows while EmpSE stays fixed. Under a correctly specified score both balancing estimators and AIPW hold near nominal coverage at every $\kappa$, while the Hájek estimator falls to between $0.07$ and $0.34$ at $\kappa = 1$. Under misspecification every estimator is biased and loses coverage as the signal grows, the balancing estimators to $0.45$ at $\kappa = 1$ for the linear outcome. The quadratic outcome is the exception, where the Hájek and AIPW estimators stay above nominal. The weights do not depend on the outcome, so the same tails apply, and under the quadratic outcome they give the Hájek estimator an EmpSE three times the linear outcome's while its bias is smaller against it.

Coverage does not change the RMSE orderings above, but illustrates how the estimators' errors would reach a confidence interval in application. For the balancing weights it is a fixed bias no variance estimator can correct, and for the MLE estimators heavy tails can widen the interval until it includes the true $\tau$. Where the signal is weak `balnet`'s bias is small against EmpSE, so a larger $\lambda$ can trade it for variance at little cost to coverage. Study 2 asks where that RMSE-minimising $\lambda$ lies inside the path, and whether any selector finds it.


```{r}
#| label: s2-helpers
#| include: false
# What the Study 2 displays have in common. All of them go through the
# three rules in s2_cell_flags() (interior optimum, selector win, lead), so
# no figure can disagree with tbl-s2-counts.

# one colour and one shape per selector, the same in every figure: the two

s2_selector_cols <- c(cv.bloss = "#2E8B57", cv.smd = "#2C5F9E",
                      boot.smd = "#9DC3E6", cv.inf = "#B2182B",
                      boot.inf = "#F4A582")

                        cv.inf = 17, boot.inf = 2)
s2_cov_labs <- c(iid = "iid", ar1 = "AR(1)", equi = "equi")

#' Theme of the Study 2 line figure, the one pn_lines() and fig_nc() use,
#' so it sits beside them.
#' @return A ggplot2 theme.
s2_theme_lines <- function() {
  theme_bw(base_size = 9, base_family = "serif") +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 10, margin = margin(b = 3)),
          plot.title.position = "plot",

          axis.text.x = element_text(size = 7))
```
