```{r}
# the noise x overlap grid, drawn in full
s2_nxo <- read_summary("cv_noise_x_overlap")

# the design columns of every cell, so the flags of s2-setup can go back on
# their grids
s2_design <- s2_grids$id |>
  set_names() |>
  map(\(id) read_summary(id)$cells |>
        select(part, cell, strength,
               any_of(c("overlap", "alpha", "n", "p", "s", "covcor"))) |>
        distinct()) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "id")
s2_flags_d <- inner_join(s2_flags, s2_design,
                         by = c("id", "part", "cell", "strength"))

#' Median lambda at which the path ends and median lambda each selector
#' picks, per overlap level: the median over a grid's cells and both arms of
#' the stored per-cell medians. The selectors never see the outcome, so one
#' pick serves every signal strength.
#' @param s read_summary() of a CV grid whose picks carry an overlap column.
#' @return Tibble: overlap, arm (the selectors and "fixed"), lambda.
s2_median_lambdas <- function(s) {
  s$picks |>
    filter(arm %in% c(s2_selectors, "fixed")) |>
    summarise(lambda = median(median_lambda), .by = c(overlap, arm))
}

#' RMSE along the lambda grid as a ratio to the endpoint's, per cell. Grid
#' points past the median lambda at which the path ends are dropped: there
#' every replication's path is already over and the ratio only repeats the
#' endpoint's. The endpoint itself is the last point, drawn at that median.
#' @param s read_summary() of a CV grid.
#' @param outcome One outcome model.
#' @return Tibble: est, overlap, strength, k, lambda, ratio, at_min.
s2_path_ratios <- function(s, outcome = "linear") {
  cells <- s$perf |>
    filter(arm == "fixed", outcome == .env$outcome) |>
    select(est, cell, overlap, strength, end = rmse)
  lambda_end <- s2_median_lambdas(s) |>
    filter(arm == "fixed") |>
    select(overlap, lambda_end = lambda)
  path <- s$perf |>
    filter(arm == "path", outcome == .env$outcome, k < 30) |>
    select(est, cell, k, lambda, rmse) |>
    inner_join(cells, by = c("est", "cell"))
  endpoint <- cells |>
    inner_join(lambda_end, by = "overlap") |>
    mutate(k = 30, lambda = lambda_end, rmse = end) |>
    select(-lambda_end)
  bind_rows(path, endpoint) |>
    inner_join(lambda_end, by = "overlap") |>
    filter(lambda >= lambda_end) |>
    mutate(ratio = rmse / end) |>
    mutate(at_min = ratio == min(ratio), .by = c(est, cell)) |>
    select(est, overlap, strength, k, lambda, ratio, at_min)
}

#' Per selector and cell of a CV grid, whether it wins against the path
#' endpoint and whether it has the lowest RMSE of the five, by the rules of
#' s2_cell_flags().
#' @param s read_summary() of a CV grid.
#' @param z Multiple of the combined MCSE a win must clear.
#' @return One row per part, cell, outcome, strength, est and selector, with
#'   ratio, the selector's RMSE over the endpoint's.
s2_selector_flags <- function(s, z = 3) {
  key <- c("part", "cell", "outcome", "strength", "est")
  end <- s$perf |>
    filter(arm == "fixed") |>
    select(all_of(key), end = rmse, end_mcse = mcse_rmse)
  s$perf |>
    filter(arm %in% s2_selectors) |>
    inner_join(end, by = key) |>
    mutate(win = rmse < end - z * sqrt(mcse_rmse^2 + end_mcse^2),
           lead = rmse == min(rmse), ratio = rmse / end, .by = all_of(key)) |>
    select(all_of(key), selector = arm, win, lead, ratio)
}

# the selector flags of every grid, with each cell's interior flag, for
# tbl-s2-selectors
s2_sel <- s2_grids$id |>
  set_names() |>
  map(\(id) s2_selector_flags(read_summary(id))) |>
  list_rbind(names_to = "id") |>
  inner_join(select(s2_flags, id, part, cell, outcome, strength, est,
                    interior),
             by = c("id", "part", "cell", "outcome", "strength", "est"))

#' Tiles of one grid: at each level of a design factor and signal strength,
#' the share of cells with an interior optimum and whether a selector wins
#' in any of them, pooled over the outcomes and the grid's other factors.
#' @param flags s2_flags_d rows of one grid, cut to the levels shown.
#' @param col Design column across the tiles.
#' @param group,sub Outer and inner strips, as plotmath.
#' @param fmt Labels for the levels of col.
#' @return Tibble: group, sub, x, strength, est, cells, interior, win.
s2_tiles <- function(flags, col, group, sub, fmt = format_plain) {
  flags |>
    arrange(.data[[col]]) |>
    summarise(cells = n(), interior = mean(interior), win = any(win),
              .by = c(all_of(col), strength, est)) |>
    mutate(group = group, sub = sub, x = fmt(.data[[col]])) |>
    select(group, sub, x, strength, est, cells, interior, win)
}

#' The dense twin's tiles, one panel per covariance structure.
#' @param flags s2_flags_d rows of one dense twin.
#' @param group Outer strip, as plotmath.
#' @return s2_tiles() rows for the three structures.
s2_dense_tiles <- function(flags, group) {
  map(names(s2_cov_labs),
      \(cv) s2_tiles(filter(flags, covcor == cv), "s", group,
                     s2_cov_labs[[cv]])) |>
    list_rbind()
}

# the panels of fig-s2-design and fig-s2-spec, in display order
s2_design_tiles <- bind_rows(
  s2_tiles(filter(s2_flags_d, id == "cv_alpha_x_overlap"), "alpha",
           "Penalty~form", "alpha", fmt_dot),
  s2_tiles(filter(s2_flags_d, (id == "cv_n" & alpha == 1) | id == "cv_nbig"),
           "n", "Sample~size", "italic(n)", format_k),
  s2_tiles(filter(s2_flags_d, id == "cv_p", alpha == 1), "p",
           "Dimension", "lasso"),
  s2_tiles(filter(s2_flags_d, id == "cv_p", alpha == 0.5), "p",
           "Dimension", "elastic~net"))
s2_spec_tiles <- bind_rows(
  s2_tiles(filter(s2_flags_d, id == "cv_noise_x_overlap"), "overlap",
           "Correct", "italic(c)", fmt_dot),
  s2_tiles(filter(s2_flags_d, id == "cv_misspec"), "overlap",
           "Misspecified", "italic(c)", fmt_dot),
  s2_dense_tiles(filter(s2_flags_d, id == "cv_sparsity"), "Denser~grid"),
  s2_dense_tiles(filter(s2_flags_d, id == "cv_sparsity_misspec"),
                 "Denser~grid*','~transformed"))

#' fig-s2-path: RMSE along the lambda path relative to the endpoint's, one
#' line per signal strength, panels by estimator and overlap, with each
#' line's minimum, the interior rule, the median endpoint lambda and the
#' median lambda each selector picks.
#' @param ratios s2_path_ratios() output.
#' @param lambdas s2_median_lambdas() output.
#' @param gain The interior rule, a dotted line at 1 - gain.
#' @param top Ratios above this are cut off, so the interior region stays
#'   readable where the top of the path is many times the endpoint.
#' @param title Title over the panels, or NULL.
#' @return A ggplot.
fig_s2_path <- function(ratios, lambdas, gain = 0.05, top = 4,
                        title = NULL) {
  c_levels <- sort(unique(ratios$overlap))
  k_levels <- sort(unique(ratios$strength))
  # plotmath strips, so c is italic as in the text
  c_lab <- \(c) factor(paste0("italic(c) == ", c),
                       paste0("italic(c) == ", c_levels))
  d <- ratios |>
    mutate(est = factor(s2_est_labs[est], unname(s2_est_labs)),
           c_lab = c_lab(overlap),
           kappa = factor(strength, k_levels, format_kappa(k_levels)))
  ends <- lambdas |>
    filter(arm == "fixed") |>
    mutate(c_lab = c_lab(overlap))
  picks <- lambdas |>
    filter(arm != "fixed") |>
    mutate(c_lab = c_lab(overlap), selector = factor(arm, s2_selectors))
  ggplot(d, aes(lambda, ratio, colour = kappa, group = kappa)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linewidth = 0.3) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 1 - gain, linewidth = 0.3, linetype = "dotted") +
    geom_vline(data = ends, aes(xintercept = lambda), linewidth = 0.3,
               linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.45) +
    geom_point(data = filter(d, at_min), size = 1.1) +
    # the picks sit on the floor of each panel, one shape per selector
    geom_point(data = picks, aes(lambda, 0.3, shape = selector),
               inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 1.6) +
    facet_grid(est ~ c_lab, labeller = labeller(c_lab = label_parsed)) +
    # the path runs left to right, from lambda_max to the endpoint
    scale_x_continuous(
      transform = scales::transform_compose("log10", "reverse"),
      breaks = c(0.5, 0.1, 0.01, 0.001, 0.0001),
      labels = c("0.5", "0.1", "0.01", "0.001", "0.0001")) +
    scale_y_log10(breaks = c(0.5, 1, 2, 4)) +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.28, top)) +
    # light for no signal, dark for the full signal
    scale_colour_viridis_d(option = "mako", begin = 0.2, end = 0.85,
                           direction = -1) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = s2_selector_shapes) +
    labs(x = expression(lambda), y = "RMSE relative to the endpoint",
         colour = expression(kappa), shape = "Median pick", title = title) +
    s2_theme_lines() +
    # two keys under the panels, one above the other
    theme(legend.box = "vertical", legend.spacing.y = unit(0, "pt"))
}

#' fig-s2-lead: the selector with the lowest RMSE in each cell, a dot where
#' a selector wins against the endpoint. Drawn as the share-of-bias heat
#' maps are.
#' @param flags s2_flags_d rows of the noise x overlap grid.
#' @param title Title over the panels, or NULL.
#' @return A ggplot.
fig_s2_lead <- function(flags, title = NULL) {
  c_levels <- sort(unique(flags$overlap))
  k_levels <- sort(unique(flags$strength))
  d <- flags |>
    mutate(est = factor(s2_est_labs[est], unname(s2_est_labs)),
           outcome = factor(outcome_labs[outcome], outcome_labs),
           overlap_lab = factor(fmt_dot(overlap), fmt_dot(c_levels)),
           kappa = factor(strength, k_levels, format_kappa(k_levels)),
           lead = factor(lead, s2_selectors))
  ggplot(d, aes(overlap_lab, kappa, fill = lead)) +
    geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.6) +
    geom_point(data = filter(d, win), size = 0.9) +
    facet_grid(est ~ outcome) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = s2_selector_cols, drop = FALSE) +
    labs(x = expression(paste("Overlap ", italic(c))),
         y = expression(paste("Outcome signal ", kappa)),
         fill = "Lowest RMSE", title = title) +
    theme_heat(length(k_levels) * 2)
}

#' fig-s2-design and fig-s2-spec: tiles of the share of cells with an
#' interior optimum, a dot where any selector wins, by signal strength and
#' the factor each grid varies, balnet on top and ABW below. Drawn as the
#' share-of-bias heat maps are, on the same fill.
#' @param tiles s2_tiles() output, panels in display order.
#' @param title Title over the panels, or NULL.
#' @return A ggplot.
fig_s2_tiles <- function(tiles, title = NULL) {
  k_levels <- sort(unique(tiles$strength))
  d <- tiles |>
    # one x level per panel column, labelled by the level alone
    mutate(x_id = paste(group, sub, x),
           x_id = factor(x_id, unique(x_id)),
           group = factor(group, unique(group)),
           sub = factor(sub, unique(sub)),
           kappa = factor(strength, k_levels, format_kappa(k_levels)),
           est = factor(s2_est_labs[est], unname(s2_est_labs)))
  ggplot(d, aes(x_id, kappa, fill = interior)) +
    geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.6) +
    geom_point(data = filter(d, win), size = 0.6) +
    ggh4x::facet_nested(est ~ group + sub, scales = "free_x",
                        space = "free_x", labeller = label_parsed) +
    scale_x_discrete(labels = \(l) sub("^\\S+ \\S+ ", "", l)) +
    scale_fill_gradient(low = "#F7F7F7", high = "#3F2A7A", limits = c(0, 1),
                        breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1), labels = c("0", ".5", "1"),
                        name = "Share with an\ninterior optimum",
                        guide = guide_colourbar(title.position = "top",
                                                title.hjust = 0)) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = expression(paste("Outcome signal ", kappa)),
         title = title) +
    theme_heat(length(k_levels) * 2) +
    theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 8))
}

#' tbl-s2-selectors: per selector, the share of cells over all grids in
#' which it wins against the endpoint, in which it wins among the cells with
#' an interior optimum, and in which it has the lowest RMSE of the five, and
#' its mean RMSE change against the endpoint (geometric mean of the ratio over
#' all cells, as a percentage), for balnet and ABW.
#' @param sel s2_sel: the selector flags of every grid with each cell's
#'   interior flag.
#' @param font Font stack.
#' @return A gt table.
table_s2_selectors <- function(sel, font = font_serif) {
  rows <- sel |>
    # given first: summarise() would otherwise read the overwritten win
    summarise(given = 100 * mean(win[interior]), win = 100 * mean(win),
              lead = 100 * mean(lead),
              gm = 100 * (exp(mean(log(ratio))) - 1), cells = n(),
              .by = c(selector, est)) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = est,
                values_from = c(win, given, lead, gm, cells)) |>
    arrange(match(selector, s2_selectors)) |>
    mutate(criterion = paste0("`", sub("^.*\\.", "", selector), "`"),
           scoring = if_else(startsWith(selector, "cv"),
                             "Cross-validation", "Bootstrap"),
           selector = paste0("`", selector, "`"))
  cells <- unique(c(rows$cells_ipw, rows$cells_abw))
  stopifnot(length(cells) == 1)
  rate_cols <- c("win_ipw", "win_abw", "given_ipw", "given_abw",
                 "lead_ipw", "lead_abw", "gm_ipw", "gm_abw")
  rows |>
    select(selector, criterion, scoring, all_of(rate_cols)) |>
    gt() |>
    tab_spanner("Selector win (%)", c(win_ipw, win_abw)) |>
    tab_spanner("Win given an interior optimum (%)",
                c(given_ipw, given_abw)) |>
    tab_spanner("Lowest RMSE (%)", c(lead_ipw, lead_abw)) |>
    tab_spanner("Mean RMSE change (%)", c(gm_ipw, gm_abw)) |>
    cols_label(.list = c(
      list(selector = "Selector", criterion = "Criterion",
           scoring = "Scoring"),
      set_names(as.list(rep(unname(s2_est_labs), 4)), rate_cols)
    )) |>
    fmt_markdown(c(selector, criterion)) |>
    fmt_number(all_of(rate_cols), decimals = 0) |>
    cols_align("left", c(selector, criterion, scoring)) |>
    cols_align("right", all_of(rate_cols)) |>
    style_booktabs(font) |>
    tab_source_note(md(paste(
      "Shares of the", cells, "cells per estimator over the ten Study 2",
      "grids. Selector win: RMSE below the endpoint's by more than three",
      "times their combined MCSE. Lowest RMSE: lowest of the five in the",
      "cell, whether or not it wins. Mean RMSE change: geometric mean of",
      "the selector's RMSE over the endpoint's, all cells.")))
}

#' tbl-s2-alpha: per penalty form, the share of cells with an interior
#' optimum and with a selector win, and the RMSE at the endpoint and at the
#' path minimum relative to the lasso's in the same cell, as a geometric
#' mean over the cells at poor overlap and full signal. The forms do not
#' share draws, so the ratios carry no paired MCSE.
#' @param flags s2_flags_d rows of the penalty-form grid.
#' @param font Font stack.
#' @return A gt table.
table_s2_alpha <- function(flags, font = font_serif) {
  key <- c("overlap", "strength", "outcome", "est")
  geo_mean <- \(r) exp(mean(log(r)))
  to_lasso <- flags |>
    inner_join(filter(flags, alpha == 1) |>
                 select(all_of(key), end_lasso = end, min_lasso = path_min),
               by = key) |>
    mutate(end = end / end_lasso, min = path_min / min_lasso)
  at_one <- to_lasso |>
    filter(overlap <= 0.25, strength == 1) |>
    summarise(end = geo_mean(end), min = geo_mean(min), .by = c(alpha, est)) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = est, values_from = c(end, min))
  shares <- flags |>
    summarise(interior = 100 * mean(interior), win = 100 * mean(win),
              .by = c(alpha, est)) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = est, values_from = c(interior, win))
  # for the note: the endpoint gain with no signal, the same for both
  # estimators, and how far any form strays from the lasso at c = 1
  no_signal <- to_lasso |>
    filter(overlap <= 0.25, strength == 0, alpha < 1) |>
    summarise(end = geo_mean(end), .by = alpha)
  at_good <- to_lasso |>
    filter(overlap == 1, alpha < 1) |>
    summarise(end = geo_mean(end), min = geo_mean(min), .by = c(alpha, est))
  rows <- shares |>
    inner_join(at_one, by = "alpha") |>
    arrange(desc(alpha)) |>
    mutate(alpha = case_when(alpha == 1 ~ "1 (lasso)",
                             alpha == 0 ~ "0 (ridge)",
                             .default = format_plain(alpha))) |>
    select(alpha, interior_ipw, interior_abw, win_ipw, win_abw,
           end_ipw, end_abw, min_ipw, min_abw)
  gt(rows) |>
    tab_spanner("Interior optimum (%)", c(interior_ipw, interior_abw)) |>
    tab_spanner("Selector win (%)", c(win_ipw, win_abw)) |>
    tab_spanner("RMSE / lasso, endpoint", c(end_ipw, end_abw)) |>
    tab_spanner("RMSE / lasso, optimum", c(min_ipw, min_abw)) |>
    cols_label(alpha = md("$\\alpha$"), interior_ipw = "balnet",
               interior_abw = "ABW", win_ipw = "balnet", win_abw = "ABW",
               end_ipw = "balnet", end_abw = "ABW", min_ipw = "balnet",
               min_abw = "ABW") |>
    fmt_number(c(interior_ipw, interior_abw, win_ipw, win_abw),
               decimals = 0) |>
    fmt_number(c(end_ipw, end_abw, min_ipw, min_abw), decimals = 2) |>
    cols_align("left", alpha) |>
    cols_align("right", -alpha) |>
    style_booktabs(font) |>
    tab_source_note(md(sprintf(paste(
      "Shares over the 84 cells per $\\alpha$ and estimator (four overlaps,",
      "seven $\\kappa$, three outcomes). Ratios: geometric mean over the 18",
      "cells at $c \\le 0.25$ and $\\kappa$ = 1 of the RMSE at the endpoint,",
      "or at the path minimum, to the lasso's in the same cell. The",
      "endpoints differ by construction and the forms do not share draws.",
      "With no signal every $\\alpha < 1$ lowers the endpoint RMSE of both",
      "estimators by %s%% to %s%%, and at $c$ = 1 every form stays within",
      "%s%% of the lasso at both points."),
      round(100 * (1 - max(no_signal$end))),
      round(100 * (1 - min(no_signal$end))),
      ceiling(100 * max(abs(c(at_good$end, at_good$min) - 1))))))
}

s2_path_cap <- paste(
  "RMSE along the $\\lambda$ path relative to the endpoint, by $c$ and",
  "$\\kappa$, linear outcome, $n$ = 1000, $p$ = 50. Points mark each minimum,",
  "the dotted line the interior rule, the dashed line the median endpoint",
  "$\\lambda$ and symbols each selector's median $\\lambda$. Ratios above 4",
  "are cut off.")
```

## Overview

@tbl-s2-counts shows how often the RMSE-minimising $\lambda$ comes before the path endpoint and how often a selector improves on it. As expected, both become more common at weaker outcome signals, where the endpoint's cost in variance stays fixed by noise while the bias it removes falls with the signal. With no signal both estimators have an interior optimum in every cell, in line with Study 1. From $\kappa = 1/4$ the two diverge, with `balnet`'s share falling from $35\%$ to $8\%$ at full signal while ABW's holds near $60\%$. On average across our outcome signal levels, an interior optimum occurs in $61\%$ of cells for `balnet` and $79\%$ for ABW.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-s2-counts
#| tbl-cap: "Interior optima and selector wins for balnet and ABW, (A) by grid, (B) by $\\kappa$."
#| tbl-pos: "!htbp"
#| echo: false
table_s2_counts(s2_flags)
```

At least one selector improves on the endpoint in $58\%$ of cells for `balnet` and $78\%$ for ABW, almost always where an interior optimum exists. `cv.bloss` wins most often for both estimators, followed by `boot.inf` (@atbl-s2-selectors). Still, none of the five has the lowest RMSE in more than around $30\%$ of cells. Applied naively, however, `boot.inf` appears the stronger candidate for `balnet`, with RMSE on average $5\%$ below the endpoint's over all settings against $1\%$ for `cv.bloss`. For ABW the two are level on average, at $15\%$ and $16\%$, so `cv.bloss` remains our choice on its win count.

## Outcome signal and overlap

```{r}
#| label: fig-s2-path
#| fig-cap: !expr s2_path_cap
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.0
#| echo: false
fig_s2_path(s2_path_ratios(s2_nxo, "linear"), s2_median_lambdas(s2_nxo),
            title = "RMSE relative to the endpoint")
```

**Interior optima:** @fig-s2-path traces RMSE along the path relative to the endpoint by overlap and outcome signal. We find that the outcome signal decides whether `balnet` has an interior optimum, while overlap sets how far below the endpoint's RMSE it lies and how strong a signal it survives. With no signal the path minimum lies $65\%$ below the endpoint at $c = 0.15$ against $17\%$ at $c = 1$, the larger gain under limited overlap we anticipated [@wang2020]. This gain closes as the signal grows, first at $c = 1$, where interior optima vanish from $\kappa = 1/8$, and everywhere by full signal. Under practical violations of common support, however, interior optima vanish sooner, lasting to $\kappa = 1/2$ at $c = 0.5$ but not at $c \le 0.25$. There the path already stops short of exact balance, so the endpoint weights are already approximately balanced and a larger $\lambda$ has little left to gain for `balnet`. This suggests $\lambda$ selection pays most in between, where the path reaches exact balance but overlap is limited.

For ABW the roles reverse, and overlap rather than signal largely decides whether an interior optimum exists. At $c \le 0.5$ it has one at every signal level, in all but one cell, while at $c = 1$ its optima vanish from $\kappa = 1/8$, as with `balnet`. Both estimators share the weights, so a larger $\lambda$ lowers the variance of both, and in every interior cell the variance falls at the path minimum. In an augmented estimator, however, the bias from the remaining imbalance scales with the error of the outcome model rather than with the outcome coefficients themselves [@athey2018]. At full signal the optimal $\lambda$ of ABW adds only $13\%$ to $16\%$ of the bias it adds to `balnet` for the linear and exponential outcomes.[^10] Here, at $c \le 0.5$ the variance saved outweighs the bias added, while at $c = 1$ there is limited variance to remove. $\lambda$ selection for ABW therefore pays wherever overlap is degraded.

[^10]: For the quadratic outcome at full signal and $c \le 0.25$, a larger $\lambda$ adds no bias to ABW, and at $c = 0.15$ lowers it, since balance on $X$ does not guarantee unbiasedness for an outcome that is not a linear function of $X$ [@zhao2019].

```{r}
#| label: fig-s2-lead
#| fig-cap: "Selector with the lowest RMSE per cell by $c$ and $\\kappa$, $n$ = 1000, $p$ = 50. A dot marks a win against the endpoint."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| echo: false
fig_s2_lead(filter(s2_flags_d, id == "cv_noise_x_overlap"),
            title = "Selector with the lowest RMSE")
```

**Selector wins:** @fig-s2-lead marks the selector with the lowest RMSE in each cell and whether it beats the endpoint. At $\kappa = 0$ every selector improves on the endpoint of `balnet` at $c \le 0.5$, and `cv.smd` has the lowest RMSE in every cell. As the signal grows the lead passes to `cv.bloss` and `boot.inf`, the only two still beating the untuned estimators in most cells at $\kappa = 1/8$. By $\kappa = 1/4$ only `boot.inf` wins, in the three cells at $c = 0.5$. This is consistent with findings from @tan2017, where cross-validating this loss beat unpenalised calibration for pure noise but lost under the linear outcome we share, as the penalty it keeps biases the fit along the covariate the outcome loads on most. For ridge-augmented linear balancing weights, @brunssmith2025 found cross-validating imbalance the best selector and cross-validating the balancing loss itself the worst. Here, we find under lasso-penalised logistic weights the order reverses, with `cv.bloss` winning in all nine cells for ABW at full signal and $c \le 0.5$ while `cv.smd` and `cv.inf` lead only with little or no signal. Whether the weights' form or the penalty drives the reversal is beyond our design.

The selectors use only the covariates and treatment, so the $\lambda$ each picks does not change with the outcome signal. The RMSE-minimising $\lambda$, however, falls as the signal grows, approaching the endpoint for `balnet` and settling above it for ABW (@fig-s2-path). Selector wins are therefore confined to the signal level where the RMSE-minimising $\lambda$ passes the one a selector picks.

Scored by the bootstrap rather than cross-validation, the same imbalance criterion selects better balanced covariates. This is most pronounced under good overlap, where `boot.smd` and `boot.inf` set $\lambda \approx 0.01$ at $c = 1$ against $0.14$ to $0.62$ for `cv.smd` and `cv.inf` at every overlap. Under good overlap the weights near the endpoint are likely robust to resampling, while under poor overlap they rest on a few units with extreme weights, so the bootstrap selects a larger $\lambda$. Over all grids bootstrapping wins on `inf` in $52\%$ of cells for `balnet` and $70\%$ for ABW, against $43\%$ and $55\%$ for cross-validation, while on `smd` both methods perform similarly (@atbl-s2-selectors). The difference lies mostly where the endpoint is optimal. There cross-validation performs far worse, with RMSE around three times the endpoint's for `balnet` at $c = 0.5$, while the bootstrap stays within about a tenth of it under good overlap. This suggests bootstrapping is the safer scoring across criteria, though `cv.bloss` remains the selector that wins most often.

**In other settings:** The remaining grids repeat this pattern (Appendix I). The penalty form matters mainly under poor overlap, where every $\alpha < 1$ improves the endpoint of ABW at every signal level while the lasso stays best for `balnet` at full signal (@atbl-s2-alpha). Along $n$ and $p$ interior optima follow how far the path stops short of exact balance, rising with $n$ at poor overlap and retreating to weak signal as $p$ grows (@afig-s2-design). Misspecification leaves `balnet` almost unchanged and removes most of ABW's full-signal optima, and in the denser grid ABW keeps a full-signal optimum in every cell only under equicorrelation (@afig-s2-spec). In no grid does a selector beat the endpoint of `balnet` at full signal under the lasso, and under good overlap neither estimator gains from approximate balance at full signal.

# Conclusion

```{r}
#| label: concl-data
#| include: false
# the five grids of the Study 1 results, their specifications pooled, read
# from the summaries the sections above already loaded; the pairs are the
# ones the conclusion quotes
concl_grids <- list("Sample size" = n_both, "Overlap" = overlap,
                    "Dimension" = p_axis, "Denser confounders" = sparsity,
                    "Outcome signal" = signal)
concl_pairs <- tribble(
  ~A,            ~B,
  "balnet0",     "glmnetcv_hajek",
  "balnet0",     "aipw_glmnetcv",
  "abw_balnet0", "balnet0",
  "abw_balnet0", "aipw_glmnetcv"
)
# the numbers the first two paragraphs quote; the render stops here if the
# stored averages no longer give them
concl_r <- \(s, A, B) s$avg |>
  filter(set == "all", block == "both", outcome == "pooled", theta == "pair",
         .data$A == .env$A, .data$B == .env$B) |>
  pull(R_bar)
stopifnot(
  isTRUE(all.equal(concl_r(n_both, "balnet0", "glmnetcv_hajek"), 68.6,
                   tolerance = 0.001)),
  isTRUE(all.equal(concl_r(signal, "balnet0", "glmnetcv_hajek"), 34.2,
                   tolerance = 0.002)),
  isTRUE(all.equal(concl_r(n_both, "abw_balnet0", "aipw_glmnetcv"), 33.8,
                   tolerance = 0.002)),
  concl_r(p_axis, "abw_balnet0", "aipw_glmnetcv") < 20,
  concl_r(sparsity, "abw_balnet0", "aipw_glmnetcv") < 20)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-concl
#| tbl-cap: "$\\bar R(\\Theta)$ of A against B over every cell of each Study 1 grid, both specifications."
#| tbl-pos: "!htbp"
#| echo: false
table_rbar_grids(concl_grids, concl_pairs,
                 note = paste("Cells: design cells × three outcomes × two",
                              "specifications; on the denser grid the",
                              "misspecification is Tan's transformation."))
```

**Across the comparable cells of Study 1,** balancing weights have lower RMSE than MLE weights in nearly every setting, alone and augmented, under both propensity scores and every outcome function, with two exceptions. Firstly, in the eight noisiest cells under a correctly specified score, the Hájek estimator has lower RMSE than `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$, as exact balance there costs more in variance than it removes in bias. Secondly, between the augmented estimators, AIPW is also level with or ahead of ABW where common support is almost certainly violated under a misspecified score and a nonlinear outcome. Elsewhere, `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ leads the Hájek estimator by between a third and two thirds on average across the grids (@tbl-concl).

Augmentation narrows the lead, to under a fifth for ABW over AIPW on the dimension and denser grids, and misspecification widens ABW's lead on every grid but the denser one. Between the unaugmented `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ and AIPW, the performance ordering depends on whether the path reaches exact balance. Where it stops short, from $p/n = 0.5$ and at $c \le 0.25$, AIPW is generally ahead. Where it reaches exact balance, `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ generally has lower RMSE, more so under misspecification. Augmentation therefore restores the lead of balancing weights wherever exact balance fails.

As the sample grows, balancing weights stay ahead of MLE weights from $n = 250$ to $10^6$, and the misspecified ordering @tan2020a report at $n \le 800$ holds to $n = 10^6$. What changes with $n$ is how each approach fails. The balancing weights converge to a fixed bias, which a misspecified outcome model cannot remove, as ABW reduces to OLS on $\tilde X$ at exact balance [@brunssmith2025]. The MLE weights never settle, as their tails lengthen with $n$, extending to $n = 10^6$ the worsening @testa2026 saw at $n = 1000$. At the empirical SE this generally leaves the balancing estimators with no coverage by $n = 10{,}000$ and the MLE estimators with nominal coverage carried by their tails, so each fails to produce reliable intervals for different reasons.

Under degrading overlap ABW separates from `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ only where its path stops short, and more data pushes that point to poorer overlap. This is consistent with the reasoning @athey2018 provide for the lead of AIPW over their approximate balancing weights. We find under misspecification the lead of `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ over AIPW also extends to poorer overlap levels. Where common support is almost certainly violated, ABW keeps most of its coverage under a correctly specified score, while `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ and the Hájek estimator have none and AIPW keeps it only for the quadratic outcome. Regardless, nominal coverage does not make an estimator reliable in this setting. At the weakest overlap under misspecification no weighting estimator removes half the confounding, as in @keele2025. There the lowest RMSE does not improve with $n$. Here applied researchers may instead consider changing their estimand.

As more covariates are considered, `balnet` becomes an approximate balancing weight from $p/n = 0.5$. Here the error of `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ becomes bias-driven and its lead over the Hájek estimator narrows with $p$, consistent with the findings of @athey2018. Misspecification costs the MLE estimators less as $p$ grows, so under it the lead of ABW over AIPW narrows, as the bias of ABW grows faster once the path stops short while the variance of AIPW falls. In @athey2018 that lead held steady under misspecification, but their models are misspecified through one covariate only, whereas we misspecify through every confounder in $\tilde X$. To our knowledge, no previous simulation has taken lasso-penalised balancing weights and cross-validated lasso MLE weights, alone and augmented, past $p = n$ under both a correct and a misspecified propensity score.

With the number of active confounders $s$ increasing, unaugmented balancing weights keep their lead at every $s$, $\nu$ and covariance structure under both scores. Under independent and AR(1)-correlated covariates their lead widens with $s$ while exact balance holds, as `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ stays close to unbiased and the error of the MLE weights grows with the number of active covariates [@tan2020b]. Once the path stops short, we find ABW's lead over AIPW grows with $s$ and the unaugmented `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ catches AIPW by $s = 64$. Under equicorrelation, where every covariate shares a common factor, the MLE bias falls with $s$ and the lead narrows at exact balance. Under Tan's transformation misspecification narrows the lead of balancing weights only while exact balance holds, as balancing a growing number of transformed covariates does not guarantee balance on the true ones.

As the outcome signal weakens, the ranking of the unaugmented estimators reverses, and in the noisiest cells under a correctly specified score `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ has higher RMSE than the Hájek estimator. Exact balance leaves it a smaller effective sample size, and the bias it removes falls with the signal, so its efficiency advantage holds only once the signal clears the noise. Under misspecification it stays ahead at every noise level but the highest.

**Our second study finds that approximate balance**, a $\lambda$ before the endpoint of `balnet`'s path, lowers RMSE below the endpoint in $61\%$ of cells for `balnet` and $79\%$ for ABW. We also find that tuning captures this gain in almost every such cell, though which selector does best differs across settings and between cross-validation and bootstrapping. For the unaugmented `balnet`, both findings hold under the Wong–Chan design, the interior optimum in fourteen of fifteen matched cells and the selector win in all fifteen (Appendix H). Under our design we observe for the unaugmented `balnet` that the outcome signal decides whether approximate balance is preferable, while overlap affects the size of its advantage. At full signal it is optimal in only $8\%$ of cells, with its advantage reduced further where the path already stops short of exact balance. For ABW, overlap largely decides whether approximate balance is optimal, as the outcome model absorbs most of the bias a larger $\lambda$ adds. Across penalty forms the lasso remains the better default for the unaugmented `balnet` at full signal, while ABW improves from the elastic net to ridge, $\alpha < 1$, as overlap degrades.

Of the five selectors, `cv.bloss` wins most often for both estimators, yet no selector maintains the lowest RMSE across more than around $30\%$ of cells. When the endpoint is already optimal, tuning imbalance by bootstrap is a generally safer approach than by cross-validation. For naive application, where the outcome signal and the propensity score's specification are unknown, we recommend `boot.inf` for the unaugmented `balnet`, as it lowers RMSE below the path endpoint's by $5\%$ on average across our settings and wins against it in $52\%$ of cells. Where it loses, in $32\%$ of cells, its RMSE sits on average a third above the endpoint's, at worst more than three times as high, in the denser setting under Tan's transformation with 64 confounders and at full signal. For ABW, `cv.bloss` and `boot.inf` are level on average, so `cv.bloss` remains our choice based on its win count.

**Both studies hinge on how strong the outcome signal is against the noise.** Where it is weak, every estimator's bias is small against the noise, so approximate balance lowers RMSE and coverage at the empirical SE stays near nominal under either score. As the signal grows, exact balance becomes the better choice for the unaugmented `balnet` and under misspecification `balnet`'s bias costs it coverage. In the worst case under a linear outcome, it holds nominal coverage only to $\kappa = 0.1$ and falls from there to $0.45$ at $\kappa = 1$, where the bias is about twice the EmpSE and a correctly sized $95\%$ confidence interval would exclude $\tau$ with around $55\%$ probability. AIPW fares no better there, at $0.69$ and $0.65$ under the linear and exponential outcomes. For `balnet`, low RMSE with nominal coverage at full signal is only achievable under a correctly specified score. There both the unaugmented `balnet` and ABW keep nominal coverage at every $\kappa$ and AIPW stays within a few points. Under our design, only the Hájek estimator loses its coverage, from $\kappa = 0.2$, as the lasso penalty shrinks its propensity score and that bias does not fall with $n$.

**For applied researchers,** who can generally observe overlap but not the outcome signal, our recommendations consider the naive application of `balnet` under situations where overlap may be weak but common support is likely to hold, and where we are certain overlap is strong. We ignore settings where there are likely violations, as in these settings a reliable estimate of the treatment effect may be beyond reach.

When confident that overlap is strong, the endpoint of ABW is the choice, as the path reaches exact balance, where it equals the unaugmented `balnet`, and pulls ahead of it wherever exact balance later fails under increased dimensionality or limited overlap.

Where overlap is reduced but common support is likely to hold, the path still reaches exact balance, so ABW at its endpoint still equals the unaugmented `balnet`, but tuning can provide benefits. Our study recommends that applied researchers using `balnet` implement ABW tuned by `cv.bloss`. However, our findings are unable to establish a universally best tuning approach, which remains an open question for future research.

## Limitations

Our conclusions rest on one family of data-generating models. Within it, misspecification takes a different form on each grid, the Kang–Schafer transformations on the four-confounder grids and Tan's transformation on the denser grids. On the cells the grids share, the Kang–Schafer form costs the balancing and augmented estimators more for the linear outcome, so the two grids' misspecified results are not interchangeable. In Study 1, Tan's transformation also runs only at $c = 1$, so how it interacts with limited overlap is untested there.

Positivity holds by construction, so the violations of common support we report are inferred from how much of the score's distribution lies near the boundary rather than imposed. Our propensity coefficients are all positive and the misspecified balancing bias is negative in every cell, so its sign may differ under other coefficient patterns. The denser grids add confounders to the propensity score and the outcome together,\[\^12\] so we cannot attribute the loss of AIPW as confounders are added to its propensity model alone.

Exact balance is generally feasible only when both arms have more units than $p$ [@wager2024], so with a treated share of one half it fails from $p/n = 0.5$, and rarer treatment would bring that point earlier. The denser grids use one correlation level, $0.5$, and adjacent active covariates. They run 1000 replications rather than 10 000, and $s = 64$ is not run at $n = 500$ and $p/n = 0.1$.

The MLE weights are tuned by five-fold cross-validation of the prediction error, not of balance, and prediction-tuned lasso can over-regularise the propensity model [@wyss2026]. Part of the advantage of balancing weights in high dimensions may then reflect this tuning rule rather than MLE itself. The MLE weights are also untrimmed, unlike the scores of @athey2018. `balnet`$_{10^{-4}}$ is taken at the end of its path rather than at a tuned $\lambda$, so Study 1 compares two default practices. Where the path stops short, the stopping rule is not logged, so infeasibility cannot be separated from slow convergence.

ABW and AIPW share one lasso outcome model, tuned by cross-validation and fitted on the same data as the weights without cross-fitting, so the gains from augmentation rest on that model. ABW with an unweighted outcome model also sits outside the model-assisted theory of @tan2020b. No variance estimator is implemented for the balancing weights, so coverage is reported at the empirical SE only, the coverage of a correctly sized interval.

Study 2 runs 2500 replications per cell, 1000 at the two largest samples, so its interior optimum rule is a reporting threshold of about two Monte Carlo standard errors. The RMSE-minimising $\lambda$ is chosen on the replications it is scored on, so its advantage over the endpoint is optimistic. The selector averages weight each setting by how often our grids run it, so another mix of signal, overlap and penalty form would move them and could change our recommendation. Our selectors never see the outcome, so the outcome-based tuning that @brunssmith2025 recommend as a starting point for ridge-augmented weights is untested. The selectors use ten folds throughout, with no other fold count tested. Under ridge and the elastic net the endpoint differs from the lasso's by construction, so the endpoints are not like for like. The Wong–Chan check uses `balnet` alone, the ATT and 1000 replications.

Future work could add a variance estimator and the coverage of its intervals, tune the MLE weights by balance rather than prediction, record why each path stops, and vary the treated share.

### Overlap levels {.unnumbered}

::: {#afig-ov-levels}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| echo: false
library(ggplot2)

# At a treated share of 0.5 the true score of DGP 2 has logit e* ~ N(0, 1/c^2),
# so everything here is exact: integrals over that law, no simulation.
# Levels: the overlap grid's seven and the n x c grid's lowest.
olev_c   <- c(2, 1, 0.75, 0.5, 0.25, 0.15, 0.05, 0.01)
olev_p   <- pnorm(qlogis(0.05) * olev_c)                 # P(e* < 0.05) = P(e* > 0.95)
olev_pct <- function(x) ifelse(x < 5e-4, "< 0.1%", sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * x))

# share of each arm in bins of width 0.1:
# P(e* in bin | W = w) = 2 * integral over the bin's logits of plogis(+/- l) dnorm(l, 0, 1/c)
olev_br   <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.1)
olev_bins <- do.call(rbind, lapply(olev_c, function(cc) {
  arm_share <- function(sgn) vapply(seq_len(length(olev_br) - 1), function(k)
    2 * integrate(function(l) plogis(sgn * l) * dnorm(l, 0, 1 / cc),
                  qlogis(olev_br[k]), qlogis(olev_br[k + 1]), rel.tol = 1e-10)$value,
    numeric(1))
  data.frame(c = cc, lo = head(olev_br, -1), hi = olev_br[-1],
             arm = rep(c("Treated", "Control"), each = length(olev_br) - 1),
             share = c(arm_share(1), arm_share(-1)))
}))

# check against the simulation code, 200 000 draws per level (e* does not depend on p)
local({
  env <- new.env()
  sys.source(here::here("R", "dgp.R"), envir = env)
  withr::local_seed(2026)
  for (cc in olev_c) {
    d <- env$dgp2(n = 2e5, p = 4, s = 4, signs = "pos", covcor = "iid", overlap = cc)
    for (w in c("Treated", "Control")) {
      emp   <- prop.table(table(cut(d$e[d$W == (w == "Treated")], olev_br,
                                    right = FALSE, include.lowest = TRUE)))
      exact <- olev_bins$share[olev_bins$c == cc & olev_bins$arm == w]
      stopifnot(max(abs(emp - exact)) < 0.01)
    }
    stopifnot(abs(mean(d$e < 0.05) - olev_p[olev_c == cc]) < 0.005,
              abs(mean(d$e > 0.95) - olev_p[olev_c == cc]) < 0.005)
  }
})

olev_panel <- function(x) factor(paste("italic(c) ==", x), paste("italic(c) ==", olev_c))
olev_bins$y     <- ifelse(olev_bins$arm == "Treated", olev_bins$share, -olev_bins$share)
olev_bins$panel <- olev_panel(olev_bins$c)
# the arms are named once, in the first panel, in place of a legend
olev_arms <- data.frame(panel = olev_panel(2), y = c(0.92, -0.92),
                        label = c("Treated", "Control"), vjust = c(1, 0))

ggplot(olev_bins, aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi, ymin = 0, ymax = y, fill = arm)) +
  geom_rect(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_text(data = olev_arms, aes(x = 0.03, y = y, label = label, vjust = vjust),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, hjust = 0, family = "serif", size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(vars(panel), nrow = 2, labeller = label_parsed) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Treated = "grey30", Control = "grey70"),
                    guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1), labels = c("0", "0.5", "1"),
                     expand = expansion(mult = 0.02)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(-1, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1),
                     labels = c("100%", "50%", "0", "50%", "100%"),
                     limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(x = expression("True propensity score " * e^"*" * (X[i])),
       y = "Share of arm in each bin") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10, base_family = "serif") +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 10),
        axis.text = element_text(colour = "black"))
```

True propensity score by arm at each overlap level $c$, as the share of each arm in bins of width 0.1. The outermost bins hold the units outside \[0.1, 0.9\].
:::

::: {#atbl-ov-levels}
```{r}
#| echo: false
library(gt)

# Levels and olev_pct() from fig-ov-levels. The share outside [d, 1 - d] is exactly
# 2 * pnorm(c * qlogis(d)); fig-ov-levels checks the law against R/dgp.R
olev_tail <- function(d) olev_pct(2 * pnorm(qlogis(d) * olev_c))

olev_tab <- data.frame(c = as.character(olev_c),
                       out_10 = olev_tail(0.10), out_05 = olev_tail(0.05),
                       out_01 = olev_tail(0.01)) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(c = md("*c*"), out_10 = "[0.1, 0.9]", out_05 = "[0.05, 0.95]",
             out_01 = "[0.01, 0.99]") |>
  tab_spanner("Outside", c(out_10, out_05, out_01)) |>
  cols_align("right") |>
  # the booktabs rules written out, so the chunk needs no handoff/ code
  opt_table_lines("none") |>
  tab_options(table.border.top.style = "solid", table.border.top.width = px(1.5),
              table.border.top.color = "black",
              column_labels.border.bottom.style = "solid",
              column_labels.border.bottom.width = px(0.75),
              column_labels.border.bottom.color = "black",
              table.border.bottom.style = "solid", table.border.bottom.width = px(1.5),
              table.border.bottom.color = "black",
              table.font.names = c("Times New Roman", "Times", "serif"),
              table.font.size = if (knitr::is_latex_output()) "8pt" else "16px") |>
  tab_source_note(md("$c$ = 0.01 is used in the $n$ × $c$ grid only."))
# in the pdf the table spans the text width, so its note lines up with it,
# and is set whole where it stands
if (knitr::is_latex_output()) {
  olev_tab <- tab_options(olev_tab, latex.use_longtable = FALSE,
                          latex.tbl.pos = "H")
}
olev_tab
```

Share of units with a true propensity score $e^*(X_i)$ outside each interval, by overlap level $c$.

### Common factor share {.unnumbered}

::: {#atbl-app-sp-share}
```{r}
#| echo: false
# the common factor's share of the propensity index's variance under
# equicorrelation, (sum_j j^-nu)^2 / {(sum_j j^-nu)^2 + sum_j j^-2nu}
share_z0 <- function(s, nu) {
  w <- seq_len(s)^(-nu)
  sum(w)^2 / (sum(w)^2 + sum(w^2))
}
tibble::tibble(s = c(4L, 16L, 64L),
               nu1 = sapply(s, share_z0, nu = 1),
               nu05 = sapply(s, share_z0, nu = 0.5)) |>
  gt(rowname_col = "s") |>
  tab_stubhead(md("$s$")) |>
  cols_label(nu1 = md("$\\nu = 1$"), nu05 = md("$\\nu = 0.5$")) |>
  fmt_number(c(nu1, nu05), decimals = 2) |>
  style_booktabs()
```

Share of the propensity index's variance carried by the common factor $Z_{i0}$ under equicorrelation, $(\sum_{j \le s} j^{-\nu})^2 / \{(\sum_{j \le s} j^{-\nu})^2 + \sum_{j \le s} j^{-2\nu}\}$.
:::

## Appendix H: Wong–Chan design {#sec-app-wc .unnumbered}

```{r}
#| label: app-wc-data
#| include: false
# Study 2's robustness check: the Wong and Chan design as Wang and
# Zubizarreta ran it, balnet only, against DGP 2's misspecified CV grid at
# matched overlap and confounding strength (stored entry wc_compare,
# handoff/R/cv.R). The captions and the Methods sentence are typed, so the
# render stops here if the stored numbers no longer match them
wc_cmp <- read_summary("wc_compare")
wc_mcse <- signif(wc_compare_mcse(wc_cmp), 2)
wc_agree <- c(interior = sum(wc_cmp$twins$interior_agree),
              win = sum(wc_cmp$twins$win_agree), pairs = nrow(wc_cmp$twins))
stopifnot(
  wc_mcse[["wc"]] == 0.085, wc_mcse[["dgp2"]] == 0.019,
  identical(unname(wc_agree), c(14L, 15L, 15L)),
  all(wc_cmp$points$m[wc_cmp$points$design == "DGP 2"] == 2500),
  all(wc_cmp$points$m[wc_cmp$points$design != "DGP 2"] == 1000))
```

The design of @wongchan2018 as run by @wang2020 has ten standard normal covariates, a logistic treatment on two, outcome model A linear in four and model B nonlinear in them, and an analyst who sees Kang–Schafer transforms of the four. We use $n$ = 5000, the ATT and 1000 replications, `balnet` balancing the covariates and their squares on a 100-point $\lambda$ grid, the logit scaled by 1, 2 or 4 and the noise SD $\sigma$ at 1, 10, 30 and 100. Cells match DGP 2's misspecified grid on the SD of the true logit ($c$ = 1, 0.5, 0.25) and on $R^2_e$, the share of the control outcome's variance the true score explains, which neither overlap knob changes. The endpoint is the last $\lambda$ reached by 95% of replications for Wong–Chan and each replication's own last $\lambda$ for DGP 2.

::: {#afig-app-wc}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| echo: false
fig_wc_compare(wc_cmp, title = "Wong–Chan against DGP 2")
```

RMSE at the best fixed $\lambda$ (top) and of the best selector (bottom), relative to the endpoint's, against $R^2_e$ by logit SD. Wong–Chan points are model A at $\sigma$ = 100, 30, 10 and 1 (left to right) and model B at $\sigma$ = 1 (open), DGP 2 points $\kappa$ = 0 to 1 under the linear outcome.
:::

::: {#atbl-app-wc}
```{r}
#| echo: false
table_wc_twins(wc_cmp)
```

Interior optima and selector wins, each Wong–Chan cell against the DGP 2 cells bracketing its $R^2_e$ at the same logit SD.
:::
